## The State of Agentic Web Readiness 2026
URL: https://veda.ng/state-of-agentic-web-2026
Summary: An empirical audit of 50,000 global websites measuring machine accessibility, Model Context Protocol adoption, Markdown content negotiation, and crawler reachability.

The web evolved from static document retrieval to interactive web applications, and now to machine-driven protocol execution. Automated AI agents, language model answer engines, and autonomous background workers make up a growing share of web traffic. Instead of rendering pixels and scrolling menus, these machine consumers parse structured data, negotiate Markdown representations, execute Model Context Protocol tools, and interact directly with HTTP APIs.

- **50,000**: Global domains audited (veda.ng AX Scanner (Sep 2026))
- **1.42%**: Sites serving /llms.txt (Empirical 50k Corpus)
- **41.2%**: Sites blocking AI search bots via WAF (Empirical 50k Corpus)
- **0.28%**: Sites with live MCP servers (veda.ng MCP Probe)

## From Human Interfaces to Machine Protocols

For thirty years, digital platform design focused on human perception. Layouts, visual hierarchy, typography, and interactive controls were engineered to hold human attention and guide manual cursor movements. That architectural model assumed a human reader was always behind the browser.

Machine consumers operate under different constraints. Autonomous agents do not scroll, view image banners, or interpret visual layout cues. They require explicit semantic declarations, deterministic URL contracts, machine-readable manifests, and typed execution interfaces. When an automated agent attempts to interact with a traditional web application, it encounters layout noise, JavaScript hydration bottlenecks, anti-bot security challenges, and unstructured HTML payloads that increase token consumption and cause execution errors.

This research paper provides an empirical assessment of website readiness for machine consumers. Using the veda.ng Agentic Scanner engine, we audited 50,000 global domains across six functional layers: Discovery, Access, Usability (MCP), Security, SEO & Citations, and Micropayments.

## Empirical Methodology

The audit corpus of 50,000 domains was constructed from five representative sectors:

1. **Top Global Domains (15,000)**: Sampled from the Tranco and Chrome User Experience (CrUX) top domain datasets to establish a general web baseline.
2. **Developer & SaaS Platforms (15,000)**: Selected from public software repositories, developer tool catalogs, and API registries.
3. **E-Commerce & Retail Platforms (10,000)**: Sampled across major commercial storefronts and digital marketplaces.
4. **Publishers & News Outlets (5,000)**: Selected from global digital publishers, research repositories, and media organisations.
5. **Emerging Tech & Web3 Protocols (5,000)**: Sampled from AI product directories and decentralized protocol registries.

Each domain was subjected to 35 asynchronous parallel HTTP probes evaluating 61 deterministic rules. Probes measured server responses for protocol manifests (`/robots.txt`, `/llms.txt`, `/.well-known/api-catalog`, `/.well-known/agents.json`, `/.well-known/mcp`), Content-Type headers under `Accept: text/markdown` negotiation, response behavior under simulated AI bot User-Agents (`GPTBot`, `ClaudeBot`, `PerplexityBot`), JSON-LD schema graphs, security header configurations, and machine payment protocols.

## Findings Across the Six AX Layers

### 1. Discovery Layer

The Discovery Layer measures whether machine consumers can locate a domain's capabilities, terms of use, and content maps without requiring unstructured crawling.

- **AI Crawler Directives in robots.txt**: 68.4% of audited domains publish a valid `/robots.txt` file per RFC 9309. However, only 12.1% include explicit directives for dedicated AI answer engine bots (`GPTBot`, `ClaudeBot`, `PerplexityBot`, `OAI-SearchBot`, `Google-Extended`).
- **llms.txt Catalog Adoption**: 1.42% of domains (710 of 50,000) serve a valid `/llms.txt` file at the domain root or `/.well-known/llms.txt`. Adoption is concentrated in Developer Tools (8.6%) and AI Platforms (14.2%), while general web adoption remains below 0.2%.
- **IETF API Catalog (RFC 9727)**: 0.18% of domains publish an API catalog at `/.well-known/api-catalog`.
- **Machine Manifests (`agents.json` & ARD)**: 0.34% of domains publish `/.well-known/agents.json` or `/.well-known/ard.json` manifests declaring operational capabilities and task boundaries.

### 2. Access Layer

The Access Layer evaluates whether automated agents can retrieve readable content without encountering security blockades or excessive token overhead.

- **Markdown Content Negotiation**: When presented with an HTTP header of `Accept: text/markdown`, 98.1% of servers return standard HTML document trees. Only 1.9% of audited domains implement content negotiation to return clean Markdown. Serving raw HTML forces agents to process layout markup, inline CSS, and JavaScript bundles, increasing average token consumption by 84.3% per request.
- **Markdown URL Twins**: 2.4% of domains expose direct static `.md` file mirrors (such as `/index.md` or `/.well-known/mcp.md`) alongside primary HTML pages.
- **WAF and User-Agent Interception**: 41.2% of domains issue HTTP 403 Forbidden, 503 Service Unavailable, or JavaScript CAPTCHA challenges when probed with standard AI search bot User-Agents (`GPTBot/1.0` or `PerplexityBot/1.0`). This occurs primarily due to default Web Application Firewall (WAF) rule sets that treat AI search bots as malicious web scrapers.
- **Server-Side Rendering (SSR) Fallback**: 18.7% of audited web applications rely entirely on client-side JavaScript rendering, returning an empty HTML shell (``) to HTTP clients. Autonomous agents that lack full browser rendering engines fail to extract content from these pages.

### 3. Usability & MCP Layer

The Usability Layer assesses a site's ability to expose interactive tools, structured API contracts, and typed machine execution surfaces.

- **Model Context Protocol (MCP) Server Exposure**: 0.28% of domains (140 of 50,000) expose a live Model Context Protocol server over Streamable HTTP at `/.well-known/mcp` or `/api/mcp`. When probed with a JSON-RPC 2.0 `initialize` request, 82.1% of these active MCP endpoints returned valid capability declarations.
- **OpenAPI 3.1 Specifications**: 4.8% of developer and SaaS domains serve an OpenAPI schema at `/openapi.json` or `/.well-known/openapi.json`. Of those, 31.4% include concrete request and response parameter examples, which are necessary for language models to construct valid API payloads without schema guesswork.
- **Machine Authentication Standards**: 1.1% of domains publish an authentication guide at `/auth.md` or expose RFC 9728 OAuth protected resource metadata at `/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource`.

### 4. Security Layer

The Security Layer evaluates network transport security, resource integrity, and vulnerability disclosure contracts.

- **HTTPS & TLS Enforcement**: 96.8% of audited domains enforce HTTPS connections across all public endpoints.
- **HSTS Preload**: 24.3% of domains issue a `Strict-Transport-Security` header matching the preload standard (`max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload`).
- **Content Security Policy (CSP)**: 19.4% of domains enforce a valid `Content-Security-Policy` header.
- **MIME Sniffing Protection**: 58.2% of domains include `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`.
- **Security Vulnerability Contact (RFC 9116)**: 6.2% of domains publish a vulnerability disclosure file at `/.well-known/security.txt`.

### 5. SEO & Citation Layer

The Citation Layer measures structured semantic annotations that allow answer engines to ground facts and attribute sources accurately.

- **JSON-LD Entity Graphs**: 44.1% of audited pages include structured data via `<script type="application/ld+json">`. However, only 14.3% declare a connected `@graph` array linking `Organization`, `WebSite`, and `Article` entities.
- **E-E-A-T Identity Signals**: 18.2% of content pages include verifiable `sameAs` links pointing to authoritative author profiles, social registries, or academic identifiers.
- **Heading Outline Hierarchy**: 62.4% of HTML documents maintain a structured heading sequence (`h1` followed by nested `h2` and `h3` tags). The remaining 37.6% skip heading levels or use multiple `h1` elements per document.

### 6. Micropayments & Machine Commerce Layer

The Payments Layer checks for standardized machine transaction protocols that allow autonomous agents to purchase metered API access or pay for computational resources.

- **Machine Payment Protocols**: 0.04% of domains advertise machine payment support via HTTP 402 headers, L402 Lightning macaroons, x402 payment headers, or Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP) manifests.

## Industry Sector Comparison

Agentic readiness scores vary across market sectors:

| Sector | Average AX Score (0-100) | `/llms.txt` Adoption | Live MCP Exposure | Markdown Negotiation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Developer Tools & Infrastructure** | **68.4 / 100** | 8.6% | 1.84% | 7.2% |
| **AI Platforms & Research** | **74.2 / 100** | 14.2% | 2.10% | 9.4% |
| **Enterprise SaaS** | **46.1 / 100** | 1.1% | 0.32% | 1.2% |
| **E-Commerce & Retail** | **31.8 / 100** | 0.08% | 0.02% | 0.1% |
| **Digital News & Publishing** | **38.5 / 100** | 0.42% | 0.00% | 0.4% |
| **Web3 & Emerging Protocols** | **52.6 / 100** | 3.8% | 0.96% | 4.1% |

Developer tools and AI research platforms lead in machine accessibility, driven by demand from software engineers using IDE agents and automated coding tools. E-commerce and general enterprise SaaS lag behind, relying almost exclusively on legacy HTML interfaces designed for human interaction.

## The Agent Readiness Framework (ARF v1.0)

Based on these empirical observations, we define the **Agent Readiness Framework (ARF v1.0)**, a standardized four-tier model for web applications:

```
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
| Layer 4: Machine Action & Payments                          |
| L402 / x402 / UCP / ACP / AP2 / Machine Terms               |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
| Layer 3: Usability & Tool Execution                         |
| Streamable HTTP MCP Server / OpenAPI 3.1 / auth.md          |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
| Layer 2: Access & Token Efficiency                          |
| Accept: text/markdown / .md Twins / SSR Fallback / Rates    |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
| Layer 1: Machine Discovery & Crawl Control                  |
| robots.txt AI directives / llms.txt / RFC 9727 api-catalog |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
```

1. **Tier 1 (Base Machine Compatibility)**: Valid `/robots.txt` with explicit AI bot rules, `/llms.txt` site catalog, XML/JSON sitemaps, and server-side HTML rendering.
2. **Tier 2 (Token-Optimised Reading)**: HTTP `Accept: text/markdown` content negotiation, static `.md` URL mirrors, and connected JSON-LD `@graph` entities.
3. **Tier 3 (Programmatic Execution)**: Streamable HTTP MCP server at `/.well-known/mcp`, typed OpenAPI 3.1 schema with parameters examples, and RFC 9728 OAuth resource declarations.
4. **Tier 4 (Autonomous Commerce)**: Standardized HTTP 402 payment challenges and machine transaction protocols.

## How India Uses AI
URL: https://veda.ng/aiindia
Summary: An analysis of AI adoption in India across consumer chat apps, public-sector backend automation, enterprise IT services, and data annotation labour.

According to [Anthropic's India Country Brief](https://www.anthropic.com/research/india-brief-economic-index), India accounted for 5.8% of global Claude.ai conversations in November 2025, ranking second worldwide behind the United States. However, when adjusted for working-age population, India ranked 101st out of 116 surveyed countries. 

Public discussions frequently conflate consumer chat applications, administrative fraud detection, weather forecasting systems, and data annotation labour into a single adoption metric, despite significant differences in underlying data sources, methodology, and measurement criteria.

![Simple three-column panel: chat apps, silent systems and model-training labour.](/images/essays/aiindia-layers.svg?v=2)

For detailed budget, GPU allocation, and fellowship data regarding the IndiaAI Mission, see [The IndiaAI Mission](/indiaai).

  - **5.8%**: of global Claude.ai use from India in Anthropic's November 2025 sample (Anthropic)
  - **44%**: of active internet users who tried AI features such as voice search, chatbots or filters in 2025 (IAMAI-Kantar)
  - **92%**: of Indian knowledge workers who said they use AI at work in 2024 (Microsoft/LinkedIn)
  - **101st**: India's Claude per-capita rank among 116 countries in the same Anthropic sample (Anthropic)

## Absolute counts and per-person ranks

The [IAMAI and Kantar Internet in India Report 2025](https://www.thehindu.com/sci-tech/technology/india-now-has-958-million-active-internet-users-57-of-these-are-from-rural-areas/article70566646.ece), presented on 29 January 2026, estimated 958 million active internet users across the country. Among respondents in the 87,000-person sample, 44% reported using AI-enabled features including voice search, image search, chatbots, and photo filters. Reported usage stood at 57% among users aged 15–24 and 52% among those aged 25–44. The broad survey definition encompasses casual product features alongside dedicated generative AI tools.

In contrast, an April 2025 [Google-Kantar study](https://blog.google/intl/en-in/products/75-of-indians-desire-a-daily-growth-collaborator-google-kantar-report/) covering 8,000 respondents across 18 urban centres found that 60% of participants described themselves as unfamiliar with AI, while 31% had tried a generative tool. Because the survey definitions, target demographics, and sampling methodologies differ substantially between these reports, their findings cannot be combined into a single unified adoption percentage.

In media interviews with the Economic Times, [WhatsApp head Will Cathcart](https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/tech/technology/for-meta-ai-india-tops-the-global-charts-will-cathcart/articleshow/131074882.cms) and [Meta CFO Susan Li](https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/tech/technology/india-is-the-largest-market-for-meta-ai-q2-profit-soars-73-at-13-billion/articleshow/112185821.cms) identified India as Meta AI's largest global market by monthly active users, though the company has not published absolute user headcounts for the region.

Google reported that the Gemini application surpassed [1 billion monthly active users globally](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/products/gemini-app/one-billion-monthly-users/) by August 2026, supported by expanded Indian-language capabilities and regional features like [Personal Intelligence](https://blog.google/intl/en-in/products/personal-intelligence-launches-in-the-gemini-app-in-india/) and [Gemini Spark](https://blog.google/intl/en-in/company-news/technology/introducing-gemini-spark-your-247-personal-ai-agent-in-country/). Google has not released India-specific breakdown figures for this global user base.

Distribution partnerships also shape surface-level reach. In July 2025, [Airtel offered](https://www.airtel.in/press-release/07-2025/airtel-partners-with-perplexity-powers-every-single-of-its-360mn-customers-with-perplexity-pro/) customers a complimentary one-year subscription to Perplexity Pro across its subscriber base. [TRAI subscription data](https://trai.gov.in/sites/default/files/2026-03/PR_No.32of2026.pdf) recorded 1,028.61 million total internet subscribers in December 2025 and [1,087.50 million broadband subscribers](https://www.gadgets360.com/telecom/news/trai-telecom-subscription-data-india-june-2026-total-subscribers-airtel-jio-vodafone-idea-bsnl-11838764) by June 2026. These telecom connection tallies and promotional bundle eligibilities reflect network access rather than active AI user engagement.

In enterprise consumer applications, [Swiggy's FY25 annual report](https://www.swiggy.com/corporate/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Swiggy-Annual-Report-FY-2024-25.pdf) details algorithmic recommendation engines and Pyng, an automated professional booking interface. Similarly, a joint report by Meta and the [Retailers Association of India](https://about.fb.com/news/2026/02/ai-fuels-indias-omnichannel-shopping-surge-meta-retailers-association-of-india/) found that 72% of surveyed digital product discovery occurred over WhatsApp. These metrics reflect automated commerce infrastructure rather than explicit consumer use of standalone AI assistants.

![Horizontal bars showing Maharashtra 15.5%, Tamil Nadu 13.2%, Karnataka 12.7% and Delhi 10.5% of India Claude.ai use.](/images/essays/aiindia-claude-states.svg?v=2)

Anthropic's telemetry data indicates that four states—Maharashtra (15.5%), Tamil Nadu (13.2%), Karnataka (12.7%), and Delhi (10.5%)—account for more than half of India's Claude.ai traffic, closely aligning with major IT services and software hubs. Software development tasks represented 45.2% of Indian Claude interactions (the highest country share in Anthropic's brief), and work-related queries accounted for 51.3% (compared to a 46% global average). This sample reflects one week of consumer Claude.ai web interactions and excludes API usage, enterprise deployments, and alternative model ecosystems.

## Public-sector deployments and backend systems

A substantial portion of AI implementation in India operates through institutional backend workflows rather than consumer-facing chat interfaces.

In a [Lok Sabha submission on 5 December 2025](https://www.mohfw.gov.in/?q=en%2Fpressrelease%2Fsteps-taken-include-ai-based-diagnostic-tools-healthcare), the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare stated that the Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS) within eSanjeevani facilitated standardised clinical data capture for 282 million teleconsultations between April 2023 and November 2025. The ministry also noted that roughly 12 million consultations received direct algorithmic differential diagnosis suggestions, alongside specialised screening tools for diabetic retinopathy and abnormal chest radiographs. Final diagnostic and prescription authority remains with the licensed medical practitioner.

The [National Health Authority's 2025–26 reporting](https://www.livemint.com/industry/nha-suspends-and-de-empanels-2-842-hospitals-for-fraud-imposes-114-06-crore-penalty-11784452386960.html) states that its National Anti-Fraud Unit used automated claim auditing algorithms to identify and block ₹678.47 crore in suspicious transactions, resulting in ₹114.06 crore in penalties across 2,842 facilities, 2,003 hospital de-empanelments, and 839 suspensions. These agency metrics do not include public assessments of false-positive claim rejections.

In agriculture, the Ministry of Agriculture reported in an [April 2025 PIB release](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2117392) that the Kisan e-Mitra multilingual conversational query system had handled over 92 lakh interactions, with daily query volumes exceeding 20,000 across 11 languages. Follow-up parliamentary data in December 2025 placed total processed queries above 93 lakh. The companion National Pest Surveillance System was deployed to more than 10,000 agricultural extension workers covering 61 crops and 400 agricultural pests.

In judicial translation, the Supreme Court's SUVAS machine translation tool processed 36,344 judgments into Hindi and 47,439 into other regional languages by March 2025, producing 83,783 translated rulings on the e-SCR portal ([PIB note, April 2025](http://www.pib.gov.in/Pressreleaseshare.aspx?PRID=2118241)). Official guidelines confirm that automated translations undergo human judicial verification prior to publication.

In meteorology, the Ministry of Earth Sciences reported in a [July 2026 Lok Sabha response](https://sansad.in/getFile/lsapps/loksabhaquestions/annex/188/AU558_ySAa9D.pdf) that the Bharat Forecast System operates numerical weather prediction at a 6 km grid resolution, delivering an estimated 30% accuracy improvement for extreme rainfall events over prior research baselines. Concurrently, a collaborative initiative involving [Google Research and the University of Chicago](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/research/indian-farmers-monsoon-prediction/) integrated NeuralGCM forecasting models with IMD historical data to deliver targeted monsoon SMS alerts to roughly 38 million farmers in 2025.

In transportation, Civil Aviation data from mid-2026 recorded over [10.75 crore biometric passenger journeys](https://www.indianaviationnews.net/home/2026/08/digi-yatra-expands-to-39-airports-over-10-75-crore-passenger-journeys-recorded.html) through DigiYatra facial recognition gates across 39 operational airports. In telecommunications, [Airtel reported](https://www.airtel.in/press-release/04-2025/airtel-announces-new-features-in-its-continued-fight-against-spam) that its network-level machine learning spam detection system had flagged 27.5 billion suspected spam calls between September 2024 and April 2025.

In financial services, the [Reserve Bank of India's FREE-AI committee](https://www.rbi.org.in/Scripts/PublicationReportDetails.aspx?ID=1306) published a governance framework outlining seven operational principles and six structural pillars for financial sector AI. In banking operations, State Bank of India leadership reported automating approximately 25% of routine cheque clearing and underwriting nearly ₹1 trillion in MSME loans using algorithmic risk assessment models in FY26 ([FIBAC coverage](https://bfsi.economictimes.indiatimes.com/articles/sbi-fully-automates-processing-of-25-of-cheques-using-ai-underwrites-nearly-rs-1-trn-in-fy26-md-amara/133177957)). [HDFC Bank's FY26 annual report](https://www.hdfc.bank.in/content/dam/hdfcbankpws/in/en/pdf/annual-reports/2025-26/reports/HDFC_Bank_IR26.pdf?outputType=chromeless) noted that its proprietary analytics platform, Neev, reduced eligibility verification latency by approximately 50% for pre-approved retail credit limits.

| Domain | Latest public record | Operational context |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Telemedicine | 282M eSanjeevani consultations with CDSS data capture to Nov 2025 | Standardised clinical record capture; doctor validates treatment |
| Health insurance | ₹678.47 Cr suspicious claims blocked in FY26 reporting | Automated fraud auditing; false-positive rates unpublished |
| Agriculture | 93L+ cumulative Kisan e-Mitra farmer queries | Multilingual voice/text query volume |
| Courts | 83,783 vernacular judgment translations by Mar 2025 | SUVAS machine translation followed by judicial review |

| Spam filtering | 27.5B suspected calls flagged by Airtel by Apr 2025 | Telecom carrier packet/call metadata analysis |

## Enterprise adoption and IT services revenue

Survey data indicates high adoption of generative AI tools among Indian white-collar employees, alongside varying rates of structured enterprise workflow integration.

The [Microsoft and LinkedIn 2024 Work Trend Index](https://news.microsoft.com/en-in/92-of-indian-knowledge-workers-use-ai-in-the-workplace-finds-microsoft-and-linkedin-2024-work-trend-index/) reported that 92% of surveyed Indian knowledge workers used generative AI tools at work, compared to a 75% global average. In [BCG's 2026 AI at Work survey](https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/tech/artificial-intelligence/india-leads-global-ai-adoption-at-work-bcg-report/articleshow/131509377.cms), 97% of Indian managers reported regular AI tool usage, with 70% of frontline users estimating weekly productivity savings of one workday. [Microsoft's 2025 report](https://news.microsoft.com/source/asia/2025/08/20/indias-workforce-goes-ai-first-as-frontier-firms-lead-the-transformation-microsoft-work-trend-index-2025/) found that 93% of Indian enterprise leaders planned to deploy autonomous AI agents within 12–18 months, with 59% reporting active pilot automation.

These figures primarily capture self-reported feedback from salaried knowledge workers in corporate environments rather than the broader labour market.

[NASSCOM's AI Adoption Index 2.0](https://nasscom.in/knowledge-center/publications/ai-adoption-index-20-tracking-indias-sectoral-progress-ai-adoption), published with [IndiaAI.gov.in](https://indiaai.gov.in/article/ai-s-presence-within-indian-organizations-has-witnessed-notable-growth-nasscom-ai-adoption-index-2-0), evaluated 500 enterprises across seven core economic sectors, assigning India an aggregate maturity score of 2.47 on a 4-point scale in 2024 (compared to 2.45 in 2022). Roughly 87% of surveyed organizations scored within the intermediate "Enthusiast" or "Expert" bands. Salesforce's [Agentic Workplace Study India](https://www.salesforce.com/in/news/press-releases/2026/07/30/india-leads-in-workplace-ai-adoption-as-workers-push-for-more-trusted-contextual-ai-experiences/) (July 2026) observed that while Indian desk workers were 45% more likely than global peers to integrate AI into daily tasks, 38% of respondents reported unsuccessful enterprise AI pilots in the preceding year (versus 28% globally), with 34% attributing pilot failures to insufficient business domain context.

![Three figures: 92% workplace AI use, 70% saving a full day, and 38% saying their organisation had an unsuccessful AI pilot.](/images/essays/aiindia-workplace.svg?v=3)

Publicly listed IT service providers have begun reporting dedicated AI contract revenues. [TCS](https://www.tcs.com/who-we-are/newsroom/press-release/tcs-financial-results-q4-fy-2026) reported annualised AI-related services revenue of $2.3 billion in Q4 FY26. [Infosys](https://www.prnewswire.com/in/news-releases/infosys-ai-revenues-at-8-2-in-q1-resilient-operating-margin-of-21-1-302833364.html) stated that AI engagements accounted for 8.2% of total revenue in Q1 FY27. [HCLTech](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/hcltech-fy26-revenue-up-3-9-led-by-increasing-demand-for-advanced-ai-302749099.html) posted annualised Advanced AI revenue of $620 million in FY26, while [Wipro](https://www.stocktitan.net/sec-filings/WIT/6-k-wipro-ltd-current-report-foreign-issuer-302c9cfab97d.html) disclosed that several hundred production AI agents were deployed across its global delivery pipelines.

![Three figures: TCS 2.3 billion dollars annualised AI revenue, Infosys 8.2% AI revenue share, and HCLTech 620 million dollars Advanced AI.](/images/essays/aiindia-services.svg?v=2)

In research talent metrics, the [Stanford AI Index 2026](https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index/2026-ai-index-report) ranked India second globally for identified AI authors and inventors (50,460 in 2025), behind the United States. Relative skill penetration among Indian LinkedIn profiles stood at 3.0 times the global baseline, while student adoption of generative AI learning tools reached 84%.

## Data annotation and human-in-the-loop labour

India remains a major global supplier of data labelling, multimodal annotation, and reinforcement learning human feedback (RLHF) services.

Industry projections by [NASSCOM](https://nasscom.in/knowledge-center/publications/data-annotation-billion-dollar-potential-driving-ai-revolution) estimate that the domestic data annotation market could reach $7 billion by 2030, employing up to 1 million full-time and part-time workers. Trade estimates cited by the [Economic Times](https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/tech/technology/indian-gig-workers-toil-at-frontlines-of-ai-revolution/articleshow/109864213.cms) indicate approximately 20,000 full-time annotation specialists working in formal facilities and over 50,000 independent contractors operating across international crowdsourcing platforms.

Field reporting from Tier-2 and Tier-3 centres highlights the operational mechanics of this sector. Accounts by [AFP](https://www.malaymail.com/news/tech-gadgets/2026/06/11/meet-the-indian-workers-training-ai-robots-to-replace-them/223341) and [TechTimes](https://www.techtimes.com/articles/324337/20260813/indian-workers-film-their-own-jobs-262-hour-train-robots-that-will-replace-them.htm) from Karur, Tamil Nadu, document Objectways technicians using wearable head cameras and smart glasses to record physical motion data for training embodied robotics models, with compensation rates around $2.62 per hour. A related investigation by the [New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/20/world/asia/ai-jobs-data-annotation-india-karur.html) detailed how distributed annotation workforces in non-metropolitan centres generate ground-truth training datasets for international foundation models.

A labour market analysis by Nomura ([Times of India](https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/business/india-business/more-hirings-than-firings-nomura-report-tests-ground-zero-says-ai-creating-more-jobs-in-india-than-cuts/articleshow/133036953.cms), [India Today](https://www.indiatoday.in/business/story/ai-creating-more-jobs-than-it-cuts-in-india-but-there-is-a-catch-artificial-intelligence-2966309-2026-08-08)) identified approximately 83,100 AI-related job additions against 31,921 AI-attributed job displacements in India between 2022 and August 2026. Hiring was predominantly concentrated in software engineering and cloud implementation roles, while workforce reductions occurred primarily within legacy customer support and routine business process outsourcing operations.

## Government infrastructure initiatives and digital public goods

Official frameworks published for the February 2026 AI Impact Summit outline the national India AI stack across compute capacity, datasets, foundational models, application interfaces, and energy infrastructure ([PIB India AI Stack Overview](https://static.pib.gov.in/WriteReadData/specificdocs/documents/2026/feb/doc202624779301.pdf), [Significance of AI for India](https://static.pib.gov.in/WriteReadData/specificdocs/documents/2026/feb/doc2026217794601.pdf)). Comprehensive compute allocations and project expenditures are tracked in [The IndiaAI Mission](/indiaai). Additional dataset catalogues on the AIKosh platform and sanctioned GPU hours were detailed in an [August 2026 PIB release](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2298788) and a [Lok Sabha submission on 5 August 2026](https://sansad.in/getFile/lsapps/loksabhaquestions/annex/188/AU2807_hKyI1X.pdf).

In education and literacy, Ministry of Education submissions to the Lok Sabha recorded [7.91 lakh secondary and 50,343 senior-secondary CBSE students](https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/india/over-8-lakh-cbse-students-enrolled-in-ai-courses-for-2024-25-session/articleshow/116143802.cms) enrolled in formal AI curriculum electives for the 2024–25 academic year, with AI skill subjects introduced in [18,839 CBSE schools](https://news.careers360.com/18839-cbse-schools-offer-artificial-intelligence-as-a-skill-subject-from-class-6-nep-2020-recommendations-education-ministry). Under the national [YUVA AI for All](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?lang=1&PRID=2214120&reg=3) digital literacy initiative, over 26.5 lakh individuals completed introductory modules by August 2026 ([TechObserver parliamentary coverage](https://techobserver.in/news/egov/indiaai-mission-gpu-hours-compute-system-lok-sabha-327929/)).

Private-public infrastructure commitments have also expanded. In October 2025, [Reliance and Google announced](https://www.ril.com/sites/default/files/2025-10/MR_Reliance_and_Google_Partner_to_Accelerate_India%E2%80%99s_AI_Revolution_across_Consumers_and_Enterprises.pdf) a strategic partnership providing Gemini model distribution across Jio platforms, Google Cloud TPU access, and enterprise solutions via Reliance Intelligence. Multi-billion-dollar hyperscale cloud and data centre investments by Microsoft and Amazon encompass broad enterprise infrastructure allocations alongside dedicated AI training and inference capacity.

Across citizen services, regional language translation relies heavily on open digital public goods, notably the Bhashini language repository. Voice-enabled agricultural advisories, multilingual land record lookups, and vernacular court document systems depend on these shared linguistic and acoustic models to function across regional languages.

## Summary of adoption dynamics

Understanding AI adoption in India requires analyzing separate, non-overlapping segments of the technology ecosystem:

1. **Consumer applications**: High aggregate conversation volumes driven by WhatsApp distribution (Meta AI) and intensive coding usage among software engineers (Claude.ai), contrasted with relatively low per-capita penetration across the broader population.
2. **Institutional public systems**: Broad-scale automated data capture and administrative rule filtering—such as eSanjeevani CDSS (282 million consultations), NHA anti-fraud screening, and DigiYatra biometric gates—operating within structured institutional workflows.
3. **Enterprise deployment**: Widespread self-reported productivity tool usage among corporate knowledge workers, balanced against measured enterprise maturity scores and ongoing challenges in business context integration.
4. **Global supply chain participation**: A substantial and geographically distributed workforce in Tier-2 and Tier-3 centres providing computer vision labelling, RLHF feedback, and motion capture data for international foundation model developers.

## Cities of India
URL: https://veda.ng/india
Summary: A government-data view of Indian cities, covering quality of life, household spending, prices and clean-air action.

India does not publish one current city score for quality of life and cost of living. The best national city ranking comes from 2020. The household spending survey covers 2023-24. The latest price data runs to July 2026. Each source answers a different question.

![A simple data panel for the Cities of India essay showing the 2020 Ease of Living score, 2023-24 urban household spending and July 2026 urban inflation.](/images/essays/india-city-scorecard.svg?v=2)

Sources are the [MoHUA Ease of Living report](https://smartnet.niua.org/sites/default/files/resources/final_web_ease_of_living_report_2020_.pdf), the [MoSPI Household Consumption Expenditure Survey](https://www.mospi.gov.in/sites/default/files/publication_reports/HCES%20FactSheet%202023-24.pdf), the [MoSPI July 2026 CPI release](https://www.mospi.gov.in/uploads/latestReleases/latest_release_1786529680747_3113661d-1a2b-4b9a-af06-b340193ef9a0_Press_Release_CPI_July_2026.pdf) and CPCB air-programme results.

  - **111**: cities in the official Ease of Living assessment (MoHUA, EoL 2020)
  - **49**: indicators across 14 categories (MoHUA, EoL 2020)
  - **₹6,996**: average urban MPCE in 2023-24 (MoSPI, HCES)
  - **3.96%**: urban CPI inflation in July 2026 (MoSPI, CPI)

## Start with the dates

The [Ease of Living dashboard](https://eol.smartcities.gov.in/dashboard) from the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs covers 111 cities. It uses 49 indicators in 14 categories: education, health, housing, water and sanitation, mobility, safety, recreation, economic opportunity, environment and resilience.

The final score gives 35% to Quality of Life, 15% to Economic Ability, 20% to Sustainability and 30% to the Citizen Perception Survey. The survey gathered more than 32 lakh responses in February and March 2020. The score therefore predates the pandemic and the last six years of urban change.

The newer sources are useful, but they do not replace the missing 2026 city ranking. MoSPI measures household spending at state level. MoSPI also measures inflation for urban India as a whole. CPCB measures air action and station-level air quality. None provides a current rent index for every city.

![Timeline showing the four dataset years: 2020, 2023-24, 2024 and July 2026.](/images/essays/india-dates.svg)

## The official ranking

[The MoHUA report](https://smartnet.niua.org/sites/default/files/resources/final_web_ease_of_living_report_2020_.pdf) gives Bengaluru 66.70, Pune 66.27 and Ahmedabad 64.87. Chennai, Surat and Navi Mumbai follow. Six cities sit within five points of each other on a 100-point scale.

Greater Mumbai ranks tenth at 58.23. Delhi ranks thirteenth at 57.56. Hyderabad ranks twenty-fourth at 55.40. The order follows the framework, city submissions, public data and citizen answers. It is not a direct vote for the city where people would prefer to live.

![Horizontal bar chart of the top ten Million-plus cities in the Ease of Living Index 2020.](/images/essays/india-ranking.svg)

The list above includes only Million+ cities. Shimla leads the separate Less than Million group at 60.90, followed by Bhubaneswar at 59.85.

The report also notes that some inputs use district or state data when city-level data is unavailable. A city score can therefore describe a wider administrative area.

## The pillars change the answer

Bengaluru tops the overall Million+ ranking because its Economic Ability score is 78.82. Its Quality of Life score is 55.67. Chennai, Coimbatore, Indore, Pune and Surat all score higher on quality.

Pune has the highest Sustainability score in the selected group at 75.74. Chennai has the highest Quality of Life score at 60.84 and the highest Citizen Perception score at 82.60. The leading city changes with the measure.

![Simple grouped bars comparing quality, economic ability and sustainability scores for Bengaluru, Pune, Chennai, Ahmedabad and Indore.](/images/essays/india-pillars.svg)

- Bengaluru leads economic ability.
- Pune leads sustainability.
- Chennai leads quality and citizen perception.
- Indore scores high on quality but low on economic ability.
- Mumbai and Delhi sit below the leaders on quality despite large job markets.

> 
The top city depends on the weight you place on work, services, air, housing and time.

## What the quality score covers

The [MoHUA report](https://smartnet.niua.org/sites/default/files/resources/final_web_ease_of_living_report_2020_.pdf) divides Quality of Life into education, health, housing and shelter, water and waste services, mobility, safety and recreation. The national average was 51.38. Safety scored 86.7 on average. Housing and shelter scored 79.5. Education scored 70.7. Recreation scored lowest.

Only 36.9% of participating cities had more than 90% of households with piped water. Many cities also had weak sewerage coverage. A score can look acceptable while a resident still faces long travel, high rent or unreliable services.

Newer sources update parts of the picture:

- The [National Health Mission](https://nhm.gov.in/index4.php?lang=1&level=0&lid=686&linkid=457) publishes health programme data to December 2025.
- [UDISE+](https://dsel.education.gov.in/en/statistics) publishes school data for 2024-25.
- The [NCRB Crime in India 2023 catalogue](https://www.data.gov.in/catalog/crime-india-2023) includes city crime tables.
- The [Smart Cities open data portal](https://smartcities.data.gov.in/) publishes city datasets for transport, health and civic services.

They do not add up to a current national city score.

## Cost of living needs a proxy

India does not publish a current official table of rent, food, transport, utilities and salaries for every city. The closest consistent measure is Monthly Per Capita Consumption Expenditure, or MPCE, from the [Household Consumption Expenditure Survey 2023-24](https://www.mospi.gov.in/sites/default/files/publication_reports/HCES%20FactSheet%202023-24.pdf). Average urban MPCE was ₹6,996.

The chart maps each selected city to its state or UT average. High spending can reflect high prices, high incomes or both. It is not a rent index.

![Horizontal bar chart of urban monthly per-person household spending for selected Indian states and union territories.](/images/essays/india-spending.svg)

Urban MPCE was ₹8,978 in Telangana, ₹8,534 in Delhi, ₹8,165 in Tamil Nadu, ₹8,076 in Karnataka and ₹7,363 in Maharashtra. It was ₹5,538 in Madhya Pradesh and ₹5,395 in Uttar Pradesh. The differences help compare household spending, but they do not price an apartment in Hyderabad or Bengaluru.

![Quadrant scatter plot comparing Quality of Life scores with urban household spending proxies for twenty Indian cities.](/images/essays/india-quadrant.svg?v=2)

The top-left quadrant contains Indore, Bhopal, Ahmedabad, Surat and Vadodara. Their quality scores sit above the sample median while their state spending proxies sit below it. Chennai and Coimbatore sit in the top-right quadrant. Cities in the same state share an x-position because MPCE is not published by city.

MoSPI’s [July 2026 CPI release](https://www.mospi.gov.in/uploads/latestReleases/latest_release_1786529680747_3113661d-1a2b-4b9a-af06-b340193ef9a0_Press_Release_CPI_July_2026.pdf) gives the current price trend. Urban CPI inflation was 3.96% year on year in July. Urban housing inflation was 2.01%.

![Horizontal bars showing urban CPI inflation at 3.96% and urban housing inflation at 2.01% in July 2026.](/images/essays/india-prices.svg?v=2)

General urban inflation rose from 2.75% in January to 3.96% in July. Housing inflation stayed near 2%. The housing index measures price change, not the rent level in each city.

## Air needs a separate chart

CPCB publishes four useful air sources:

- [National Ambient Air Quality Monitoring Programme](https://cpcb.nic.in/namp-data/) monitoring data.
- [National Air Quality Index](https://airquality.cpcb.gov.in/AQI_India/) station and city readings.
- [PRANA](https://prana.cpcb.gov.in/) National Clean Air Programme tracking across 130 cities.
- [Swachh Vayu Survekshan 2024](https://prana.cpcb.gov.in/ncapServices/robust/fetchFilesFromDrive/Swachh_Vayu_Survekshan_2024_Result.pdf) city action results.

Surat, Jabalpur and Agra lead the Million+ category in the 2024 clean-air action assessment. That result measures assessed action and PM10 improvement. It is not an annual PM2.5 exposure ranking.

![Three ranked cards showing Surat first, Jabalpur second and Agra third in the 2024 Swachh Vayu Survekshan Million-plus category.](/images/essays/india-air.svg?v=2)

## Why there is no new combined rank

A combined 2026 rank would require current, city-level measures that do not exist in one government release. The available sources use different dates and geographies.

Keep the measures separate. The 2020 score is the common city baseline. MPCE is a state-level spending measure. CPI is a current urban price-change measure. The air chart is a programme result. None is a rent quote.

## What the main cities show

### Bengaluru

Bengaluru leads the overall index because its economic score is far ahead of the field. Its quality score is lower than Chennai, Pune, Indore and several other cities.

### Pune

Pune ranks second overall and first on sustainability in the selected group. Its quality and economic scores are also above average.

### Chennai

Chennai leads Quality of Life at 60.84 and Citizen Perception at 82.60. Urban Tamil Nadu MPCE is ₹8,165, above the all-India urban average.

### Ahmedabad and Surat

Ahmedabad ranks third overall. Surat ranks fifth and leads the 2024 clean-air action assessment for Million+ cities.

### Indore

Indore ranks ninth overall and scores 59.86 on Quality of Life. Urban Madhya Pradesh MPCE is ₹5,538, below the national urban average.

### Mumbai and Delhi

Greater Mumbai ranks tenth overall at 58.23. Delhi ranks thirteenth at 57.56. Both score near the middle on Quality of Life despite large labour markets.

### Hyderabad

Hyderabad ranks twenty-fourth overall at 55.40. Telangana has the highest urban MPCE in the selected group at ₹8,978.

## What a better release would include

A current city scorecard needs one geography and one release schedule. It should publish:

1. City boundaries and the district or metropolitan area used for each measure.
2. A quality-of-life score with the year of every input.
3. Median rent by dwelling size and distance from public transport.
4. Food, fuel, electricity, water, education and health spending.
5. Travel time and transit access by ward.
6. Annual PM2.5 and PM10 exposure with station coverage.
7. Health, school and crime data with population denominators.
8. Income and employment data beside spending data.

MoHUA, MoSPI, CPCB, NCRB, the National Health Mission and the Ministry of Education already publish pieces of this system. They do not yet publish them as one current city scorecard.

## The ranking

The official answers are:

- **Overall Million+ score:** [Bengaluru, 66.70](https://smartnet.niua.org/sites/default/files/resources/final_web_ease_of_living_report_2020_.pdf).
- **Quality of Life:** [Chennai, 60.84](https://smartnet.niua.org/sites/default/files/resources/final_web_ease_of_living_report_2020_.pdf).
- **Sustainability:** [Pune, 75.74](https://smartnet.niua.org/sites/default/files/resources/final_web_ease_of_living_report_2020_.pdf).
- **Economic Ability:** [Bengaluru, 78.82](https://smartnet.niua.org/sites/default/files/resources/final_web_ease_of_living_report_2020_.pdf).
- **Citizen Perception:** [Chennai, 82.60](https://smartnet.niua.org/sites/default/files/resources/final_web_ease_of_living_report_2020_.pdf).
- **Less than Million group:** [Shimla, 60.90](https://smartnet.niua.org/sites/default/files/resources/final_web_ease_of_living_report_2020_.pdf).
- **2024 clean-air action:** [Surat](https://prana.cpcb.gov.in/ncapServices/robust/fetchFilesFromDrive/Swachh_Vayu_Survekshan_2024_Result.pdf).

Bengaluru leads the old overall index. Chennai leads quality and citizen perception. Pune leads sustainability. Surat leads clean-air action. Indore combines a high quality score with lower state-level urban spending. Hyderabad shows why a high spending level should not be read as affordability.

The next national Ease of Living release should be read beside current CPI, household spending and CPCB station data. Until then, ask which city performs well on the measure that matters to you, and how recent that measure is.

## Who Buys After the Layoff
URL: https://veda.ng/receipts
Summary: AI can cut a wage without cutting a customer, change a job, or create a new one. The open question is which of those three happens to the receipt.

On 27 February 2024, [Klarna](https://www.klarna.com/international/press/klarna-ai-assistant-handles-two-thirds-of-customer-service-chats-in-its-first-month/) said an OpenAI-powered assistant had handled 2.3 million conversations in its first month, two-thirds of customer-service chats, work equal to 700 full-time agents, and an estimated $40 million of 2024 profit improvement. The company also said customers could still choose a live agent. [American Banker](https://www.americanbanker.com/payments/news/klarnas-ai-does-the-work-of-700-people-whats-that-really-mean) later reported Klarna's own clarification: the 700 figure was an equivalent, not a same-day headcount cut, and outsourced agents could be moved to other clients. In May 2025, [Fortune](https://fortune.com/2025/05/09/klarna-ai-humans-return-on-investment/) and [Fast Company](https://www.fastcompany.com/91332763/going-ai-first-appears-to-be-backfiring-on-klarna-and-duolingo) reported CEO Sebastian Siemiatkowski telling Bloomberg that cost had been too dominant a metric, quality had fallen, and Klarna would hire humans again while still using AI.

![Three replacements for a lost wage: another job, a transfer, or an agent spending capital income](/images/essays/receipts.svg?v=2)

The public argument about AI and work is usually binary: jobs die, or jobs multiply. Neither claim matches the record as of August 2026. Some tasks are automated, some jobs change composition, and some new roles appear, especially around energy, chips, and data centers. Some entry-level hiring stalls. A wage is also a shopping budget. If the wage leaves a household faster than another budget replaces it, someone who used to buy groceries, software seats, and sneakers buys less. If a new paycheck, a transfer, or an authorized agent replaces that budget, receipts can hold even as the original job does not. The sections below check which of those three replacements the data currently support, and which they do not.

## What the numbers measure

Start with exposure, which is not the same as unemployment. [Eloundou, Manning, Mishkin, and Rock](https://openai.com/research/gpts-are-gpts) estimated that around 80% of the US workforce is in occupations where at least 10% of tasks could be affected by large language models, and about 19% in occupations where at least 50% of tasks could be. The [Science](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.adj0998) version of the same project is more conservative on "over half the tasks" once you restrict to simple LLM interfaces, then jumps when you add likely software wrappers. The authors score tasks. They do not date adoption or count layoffs.

The [IMF Staff Discussion Note SDN/2024/001](https://www.imf.org/-/media/files/publications/sdn/2024/english/sdnea2024001.pdf) by Cazzaniga, Jaumotte, Li, Melina, Panton, Pizzinelli, Rockall, and Tavares puts global employment exposure near 40%, about 60% in advanced economies, 40% in emerging markets, and 26% in low-income countries. In advanced economies they split high-exposure work roughly into 27% high complementarity and 33% low complementarity. [Kristalina Georgieva's IMF blog](https://www.imf.org/en/blogs/articles/2024/01/14/ai-will-transform-the-global-economy-lets-make-sure-it-benefits-humanity) repeats the 40% global figure and stresses that AI hits cognitive jobs, so rich countries are both more exposed and more able to use the tools. India's exposure in that note is lower than Brazil's on the country sample because of occupational mix.

Forecasts of net job change still disagree, which is a fact about models. Averaging them does not produce a better forecast. [Goldman Sachs Research](https://www.goldmansachs.com/insights/articles/how-will-ai-affect-the-us-labor-market) has used a global exposure figure of about 300 million jobs, a US estimate that AI could automate tasks equal to 25% of work hours, and a base case of 6-7% of workers displaced over roughly a decade, with unemployment up about 0.6 percentage points if the transition is spread out. Faster adoption, they say, would hit harder. The [World Economic Forum Future of Jobs Report 2025](https://www.weforum.org/publications/the-future-of-jobs-report-2025/) surveys employers and publishes a 2030 churn of 170 million jobs created and 92 million displaced, a net plus 78 million, with clerical work on the decline list and AI, data, and energy roles on the growth list. Employer surveys are not labor-force surveys. The WEF net is a stated hiring intention, not a census.

Announcement data is messier still. [Challenger, Gray & Christmas](https://www.challengergray.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Challenger-Report-July-2026.pdf) counted 33,429 US job-cut announcements in July 2026, the lowest monthly total in two years, and 477,033 year to date, down 41% from 806,383 in the first seven months of 2025. AI was the leading cited reason in July (10,970 cuts, 33% of the month) for a fifth straight month, and 112,713 year to date, about 24% of 2026 announcements. Since the firm began tracking AI as a distinct reason, the cumulative AI-cited total is 184,538. Technology still led industries (149,023 cuts in 2026 through July, 31% of the total). Andy Challenger also said hiring plans were up 25% year to date and that AI is "not dismantling" the labor market. The same report created a bucket, "Technological Update (possibly AI)," because firms allude without pinning the model. [HR Executive](https://hrexecutive.com/) quoted Avature CEO Dimitri Boylan warning that "AI" is becoming shorthand investors like. Visa's 7% reduction, in that write-up, was an efficiency story in which AI would change work. A cited reason is not a cause, and a missing citation does not mean AI was absent.

Payroll microdata is the closest thing to a current labor fact. [Brynjolfsson, Chandar, and Chen](https://digitaleconomy.stanford.edu/publication/canaries-in-the-coal-mine-six-facts-about-the-recent-employment-effects-of-artificial-intelligence/) at the Stanford Digital Economy Lab, August 2026 revision, use ADP payroll covering millions of US workers through June 2026. They report six facts. There is no evidence of economy-wide job destruction. Employment of workers aged 22-25 in AI-exposed occupations stands 19% below the path of less-exposed peers; experienced workers show no comparable gap. The gap has widened since their 2025 drafts (earlier public versions said 13%, then 16%). The channel is reduced hiring more than increased separations. Declines concentrate where AI usage substitutes for tasks; where it complements, employment is flat or rising, especially for experienced workers. Adjustment is in employment, not base pay. They flag that the pattern attenuates with education controls, that some divergence predates ChatGPT, and that ADP looks sharper than some national survey benchmarks. They call the facts canaries, not causal estimates.

That sits beside an older productivity paper. [Brynjolfsson, Li, and Raymond](https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjae044) in the *Quarterly Journal of Economics* (2025; NBER w31161) studied 5,172 customer-support agents given a generative assistant. Issues resolved per hour rose about 15% on average, with the largest gains among less experienced agents (on the order of one-third in the working-paper versions). Quality and customer sentiment moved with speed for novices. That is augmentation inside a job. The Stanford ADP paper is about whether the junior seat exists to be augmented. Both can be true in different firms in the same quarter.

The ILO's [Generative AI and Jobs](https://www.ilo.org/publications/generative-ai-and-jobs-global-analysis-potential-effects-occupational) analysis (Gmyrek, Berg, Bescond) likewise stresses occupation-level exposure and clerical concentration, not a single global unemployment rate. The [OECD Employment Outlook](https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/oecd-employment-outlook-2024_ac8b3538-en.html) line has been similar: adoption is real, aggregate employment effects through the mid-2020s are still modest, and the distribution inside occupations is the live issue. [Autor's 2015 JEP essay](https://doi.org/10.1257/jep.29.3.3), "Why Are There Still So Many Jobs?", remains the right prior: machines take tasks, remaining tasks often become more valuable, and new work appears. Whether that prior still holds is an empirical question.

## Three things can happen to a job. Only one of them is disappearance.

David Autor, Caroline Chin, Anna Salomons, and Bryan Seegmiller's [New Frontiers](https://www.nber.org/papers/w30389) (*QJE* 2024) tracks new work in US Census and SOC titles from 1940 to 2018. New occupational titles keep arriving. Demand shocks and technological complementarity create them. Automation also destroys old titles. The net has not been a one-way slide into idleness. [Acemoglu and Restrepo](https://doi.org/10.1257/mac.20161170) (2018, 2019) split the same history into displacement (automation of existing tasks) and reinstatement (new tasks for labor). They have also argued, in later work, that displacement intensified in recent decades while reinstatement did not always keep up. They are warning that displacement can outrun new tasks.

James Bessen's ATM history is the standard counterexample to "the machine ate the occupation." As [Bessen](https://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/fandd/2015/03/bessen.htm) and Autor both recount, US ATM counts rose from roughly 100,000 to 400,000 between the mid-1990s and 2010. Tellers per urban branch fell (on the order of 20 to 13). Branch counts rose enough that teller employment did not collapse; Autor cites teller employment moving from about 500,000 to 550,000 between 1980 and 2010, even as the occupation's share of all jobs slipped. The remaining job mixed less cash and more customer work. AI deployments copy that outcome only if demand for the output is elastic and the leftover human tasks are worth staffing.

Displacement, when it does happen, is expensive for the person even after reemployment. [Jacobson, LaLonde, and Sullivan](https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/aer.83.4.685) (*AER* 1993), using Pennsylvania administrative data, found high-tenure workers separating from distressed firms suffered long-term earnings losses averaging about 25% per year. Losses began before separation. They were not confined to a few industries. They remained large even for workers who found jobs in similar firms. [Couch and Placzek](https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/aer.100.1.572) (2010) revisited the result with different data; the qualitative finding, large and persistent earnings losses, survived. Unemployment insurance replaces a fraction of lost wages during joblessness. It does not restore the firm-specific component after the new job starts. For consumer demand, that gap matters. A rehired worker is not a fully restored shopper.

Historical panic is also data. David Ricardo added the machinery chapter to the *Principles* in 1821 because he changed his mind: machines could hurt labor in some cases. Keynes, in [Economic Possibilities for our Grandchildren](https://www.marxists.org/reference/subject/economics/keynes/1930/our-grandchildren.htm) (1930), coined "technological unemployment" as a temporary mismatch of finding new uses for labor. Both texts are still quoted by people who have not read the surrounding paragraphs. Ricardo was writing about whether machines could hurt labor in some cases. Keynes was writing a century-scale essay about abundance. Both are history of thought, not 2026 forecasts.

## The worker was also the customer

On 5 January 1914, Ford Motor Company announced a $5 day, up from about $2.34, with an eight-hour shift. [The Henry Ford](https://www.thehenryford.org/collections/explore/articles/fords-five-dollar-day) documents the context: assembly-line time for a Model T had fallen from 12.5 hours toward 93 minutes, turnover was extreme (the museum's artifact notes cite figures around 370-380% annually), and the raise was profit-sharing with a Sociological Department attached. Ford later called it a cost-cutting move because it bought retention. The museum also records the second-order effect Ford himself noted: better-paid workers were a pool of Model T buyers. [Kellogg's teaching case](https://www.kellogg.northwestern.edu/academics-research/research/detail/2023/henry-fords-five-dollar-day) states the same mechanism without romance. Mass production needs mass buying. If you pay the people who make the good, some of the demand is internal.

That identity is weaker in 2026 than in 1914, and pretending otherwise is propaganda. Ford workers were a visible slice of the car market. A SaaS company's support agents are a rounding error in global seat demand. A retailer that cuts store labor still sells mostly to non-employees. The identity is strongest for mass-market categories whose customers are wage earners as a class, not as badge-holders of one firm: groceries, mass apparel, fast food, consumer credit, mid-market autos, budget telecom. It is weakest for luxury and for producer goods sold to other firms.

The spending arithmetic is in household surveys, not in LinkedIn posts. The [BLS Consumer Expenditure Survey for 2024](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/cesan.nr0.htm) shows average annual outlays of $35,046 in the lowest income quintile and $150,342 in the highest, against an all-consumer-unit average of $78,535. High-income households spend more in dollars and a smaller share of income. [Fisher, Johnson, Smeeding, and Thompson](https://www.bostonfed.org/publications/research-department-working-paper/2019/estimating-the-marginal-propensity-to-consume-using-the-distributions-income-consumption-wealth.aspx) at the Boston Fed, using PSID data, find that the marginal propensity to consume is lower in higher wealth quintiles; in their summary, the MPC for low-wealth households is an order of magnitude larger than for wealthy households, and the overall two-year MPC is about 10%. [Fisher et al. (2016)](https://equitablegrowth.org/working-papers/estimating-the-marginal-propensity-to-consume/) report average propensities above 0.8 for the bottom 10% of income and below 0.6 for the top 10%. [Dynan, Skinner, and Zeldes](https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/381475) (2004) documented that saving rates rise with income. Kaldor's 1956 stylized fact, workers consume more of a marginal dollar than owners, is still the right first approximation, even if the micro estimates vary with horizon and instrument.

Move income from a junior support wage to retained earnings and three things can happen to sectoral demand. The household cuts outlays. The owners consume, but a smaller share, and often different baskets (Matsuyama's non-homothetic demand; [Comin, Lashkari, and Mestieri](https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.20171800) on income-driven demand). Or the firm invests the saving in equipment, which shows up in GDP as investment, not as the original consumer category. Any of those three can empty a particular merchant's register even if GDP holds.

Macro totals in 2026 do not show a consumption crash. They also do not show a fat household buffer. The [BEA](https://www.bea.gov/news/2026/personal-income-and-outlays-june-2026) put the personal saving rate at 2.7% in June 2026, with personal saving of $646.1 billion. The [BEA saving-rate page](https://www.bea.gov/data/income-saving/personal-saving-rate) lists March 2026 at 3.5%, April 3.0%, May 2.8%. [FRED PSAVERT](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/PSAVERT) matches those prints. The [BEA GDP advance for Q2 2026](https://www.bea.gov/news/2026/gdp-advance-estimate-2nd-quarter-2026) has real GDP up 1.5% annualized after 2.1% in Q1. Consumer spending and investment both contributed; government spending subtracted; imports rose. Real final sales to private domestic purchasers rose 3.9% in Q2 after 1.7% in Q1. Secondary write-ups of the same release (for example [this recap](https://www.thejakartapost.com/business/2026/07/31/imports-hold-back-us-economic-growth-in-q2-but-domestic-demand-robust.html)) put Q2 consumer spending growth at 3.2% after 0.5% in Q1, and equipment spending at a 15.2% pace, with AI infrastructure named as a driver. Use the BEA tables as the authority; use the recap only for the equipment color. A low saving rate plus strong equipment investment is consistent with households stretching and firms buying GPUs. It does not tell you next year's same-store sales.

[Falk and Tsoukalas](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.20617) (2026) formalize a related idea: if firms capture the full wage saving from automation and only a fraction of the lost product-market demand, competition can push automation past the level that maximizes even owners' joint profits. That model is a hypothesis about incentives. It is not evidence that US consumption has already fallen by the size of AI-cited Challenger cuts. Those cuts are still small relative to a labor force above 160 million.

## Replacement one: another human job

This is the reinstatement path. The WEF's +170 million / -92 million split is the corporate version. Challenger's 2026 hiring rebound, concentrated in what Andy Challenger called floor work (aerospace, energy, manufacturing), is a weaker, nearer-term version. Data-center construction, grid interconnection, and chip packaging are real hiring categories. They do not automatically rehire the 24-year-old who is not getting the customer-success seat. Occupation mismatch is how you get both "labor shortage" headlines and "entry-level ice" headlines in the same month.

Bessen's ATM case is the optimistic template: cheaper branches, more branches, different teller. The pessimistic template is typesetting, which Bessen also uses: desktop publishing reduced compositors and increased designers. Work moved across occupations. The people were not always the same people. Jacobson losses apply here. Even successful movers often earn less for years. For a grocer, that is a quieter customer. For a luxury house, it may be noise.

Goldman Sachs's 0.6 percentage-point unemployment bump in a slow-adoption base case is a reminder of scale. A move from the low 4s toward the mid-4s is a small change in the national rate. The Stanford 19% relative gap for young workers in exposed occupations still sits inside that average. Averages hide the first rung of the ladder.

## Replacement two: a transfer

If the wage does not come back as a wage, it can come back as unemployment insurance, SNAP, wage insurance, a negative income tax, or a dividend on a public or private claim. Each has a different MPC and a different lag. Jacobson and LaLonde were blunt in *The Costs of Worker Dislocation*: existing programs do not, and probably cannot, cover most of the loss, because much of it arrives after reemployment. A UBI, in the mechanical sense of an unconditional add-on to disposable income, raises the consumption floor. It does not, by itself, change a firm's incentive to automate the next task. Those are the cash-flow effects, whether you support UBI or not.

Worker equity is the other transfer. If displaced staff still hold stock, some profit returns to a high-MPC household. Employee stock ownership is uneven, concentrated in listed tech, and usually too small to replace a salary. Co-determination and profit-sharing have a long literature ([Weitzman 1985](https://www.jstor.org/stable/1805623) is the classic). Voluntary adoption that surrenders a large profit share is rare. Mandates are politics. The narrower claim is enough: equity can recycle some demand; it has not been shown, in US data, to recycle enough to offset a 25% earnings scar.

## Replacement three: an agent spending someone else's mandate

This is the path that did not exist as infrastructure in 2014. [Agentic commerce](/agentcommerce) is the practice of software discovering, comparing, and paying within rules a person or firm set. [McKinsey](https://www.mckinsey.com.br/capabilities/quantumblack/our-insights/the-agentic-commerce-opportunity-how-ai-agents-are-ushering-in-a-new-era-for-consumers-and-merchants) has published a 2030 range of about $900 billion to $1 trillion of US B2C retail "orchestrated" by agents, and $3 trillion to $5 trillion globally. Those are research estimates under stated assumptions about adoption and merchant readiness, not observed GMV. McKinsey's later [automation-curve](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/quantumblack/our-insights/the-automation-curve-in-agentic-commerce) note keeps the same global band.

The rails are no longer hypothetical. [Visa Intelligent Commerce](https://www.visa.com/en-us/solutions/intelligent-commerce) is a product family for agent-initiated payments with controls and tokens. Visa's [corporate perspective](https://corporate.visa.com/en/sites/visa-perspectives/innovation/agentic-commerce-expanded-payments-economy.html) cites 14,500 financial institutions and 175 million merchant locations as the network the agents would ride. Mastercard has public Agent Pay work. OpenAI and Stripe shipped an Agentic Commerce Protocol for in-chat checkout. Google has pushed AP2-style credentialed mandates and, with retailers, a Universal Commerce Protocol. Anthropic's MCP and Google's A2A are not shopping protocols; they are how tools and agents talk. Together they make it possible for purchasing power to move without a browser session.

An agent does not create a budget. It spends a budget that already exists: a wage, a credit line, a corporate treasury, a parent's card, an owner's draw. If the junior wage is gone and no transfer replaces it, the agent has nothing to spend unless capital income is assigned to it. That assignment is a distributional choice: family sharing, employer stipends, public transfers, or owners instructing agents to buy mass-market goods they themselves would not browse. Non-homothetic demand says the last of those is the least likely for groceries.

Trust is the measured brake. Earlier consumer surveys (including figures used in the [agentic commerce](/agentcommerce) essay: high use of AI tools, much lower trust to complete a purchase) should be updated as products ship, but the gap is the right object. Fraud, chargebacks, and "the agent bought the wrong SKU" are why Visa talks about tokens and mandates instead of scraping card numbers into a prompt.

There is a further mismatch of baskets. A wage-funded human buys on habit, brand, and proximity. An agent buys on constraints: price, delivery slot, spec, return rate. Merchants that spent a decade optimizing landing pages lose that surface. Merchants that publish machine-readable inventory, policy, and price may keep the ticket even if the human job that used to click "buy" is gone, provided the budget remains. Having a shopping protocol does not restore a missing wage.

## What the counter-arguments get right

First, general equilibrium. Income that leaves a call-center payroll does not leave Earth. It may appear as lower prices, higher profits, cheaper goods, and more real consumption for whoever still has a claim. If AI lowers the price of software support, users buy more of something else. That is the standard productivity defense, and it is often correct with a lag. The lag is the investigative object. Ramey and Shapiro's work on costly capital reallocation is the industrial version: factories do not instantly become other factories. Occupations do not instantly become other occupations.

Second, measurement. Challenger counts press releases. ADP is a selected payroll processor. BLS household and establishment surveys disagree with private payroll in ordinary years. Eloundou scores tasks with humans and with GPT-4; the Science and working-paper summaries do not match digit-for-digit depending on software assumptions. IMF complementarity is a constructed index. WEF is a survey of HR intentions. Goldman is a staff scenario. Anyone stacking these into one "AI jobs number" is inventing a statistic.

Third, labeling. Firms have an incentive to say "AI" when the real story is interest rates, overhiring in 2021-2022, or a failed product. They also have an incentive not to say "AI" when they fear brand damage, which is why Challenger added the "possibly AI" bucket. Duolingo's AI-first contractor policy drew public pushback; that is reputation, which can feed back into consumer demand without a single layoff showing in BLS.

Fourth, emerging markets. IMF exposure is lower where work is still manual. A layoff in Bangalore IT services is a demand event for urban consumption in India; a harvest-season labor pattern is not. The Stanford 22-25 finding is a US ADP payroll result. It does not transfer onto the Indian Periodic Labour Force Survey.

Fifth, quality reversal. Klarna's 2025 rehiring is evidence that some "700 FTE equivalent" claims were cost savings that failed a CSAT test. IBM's own survey, as cited by Fortune, found that a minority of AI projects delivered the promised return. Automation that does not stick does not remove the wage, and therefore does not remove the shopper.

## A checklist

If you run a consumer business, track three ratios.

1. What share of your category's buyers are wage-dependent in the occupations your own sector is automating? A luxury watch brand and a prepaid wireless carrier do not share an answer.
2. How fast is income replaced for those occupations in your catchment: new jobs (watch vacancies and wage offers in Lightcast or JOLTS), transfers (UI claims), or other household income (second earners, credit)?
3. If an agent becomes the buyer, do you have a product record an agent can purchase without a human landing page, and is there a funded mandate behind it?

If you run a labor ministry or a central bank, the analogous trio is: occupation-age cells (Stanford's canary), consumption by income quintile (BLS CE), and the saving rate plus equipment investment split (BEA). A calm unemployment rate with a collapsing 22-25 employment ratio in exposed jobs and a 2.7% saving rate is a different economy from a calm unemployment rate with stable junior hiring.

If you write model policy, tax the right margin or admit you are doing something else. A profit tax and a UBI can be justified on equity grounds. They do not, as a matter of first-order conditions, change the private return to automating the next task. A tax or a standard on the automation itself does. Whether that is wise depends on complementarity, measurement, and evasion. The IMF note is more useful here: prepare infrastructure and training where complementarity is high; do not pretend exposure is destiny.

## The receipt is the test

Ford paid $5 in part because turnover was eating the line, and in part because mass production without mass buying is a pile of unsold cars. Klarna published a 700-agent equivalent and then discovered that some of the demand it needed was the feeling of a competent human on the other end of a dispute. Stanford's 19% gap says the first rung is already different for a subset of occupations. BEA says households are still spending, and saving little. Challenger says firms keep typing "AI" on layoff notices even as total notices fall from 2025. McKinsey says agents might sit in front of trillions of dollars of checkout by 2030 if merchants and shoppers allow it.

AI will remove some jobs, change some jobs, and create some jobs. The proportions are not known, and anyone who states them as a point forecast is guessing. The part that can be investigated without waiting for 2030 is narrower. When a wage stops, does a receipt continue, and through which of the three pipes: a new wage, a transfer, or a funded agent. If the pipe is empty, the firm that cut the cost also cut a customer, usually someone else's, which is why the incentive to keep cutting does not police itself.

The next useful dataset is a merge of occupation-level hiring, household consumption by those occupations, and the share of checkout that arrives with a machine mandate rather than a human session. Until that merge exists, the honest position is conditional. If reinstatement is fast, the 1914 logic still holds. If transfers arrive, demand becomes a political calendar. If agents spend capital income on mass goods, the shopper is no longer the worker, and storefronts built for human habit will fail even when GDP looks fine. If none of the three pipes fill, the layoff is also a demand forecast, and it will show up first in the categories wage earners actually buy.
