## The State of AI
URL: https://veda.ng/stateofai
Summary: An OpenAlex sweep of 5,003,783 papers whose abstracts match AI method terms, 2013 through mid-2026. Neural networks still lead the cumulative count. LLM mentions grew 29.9x from 2018 to 2025. China leads volume. The US still leads LLM papers. 48.9% of the corpus has zero citations.

Five million papers. That is the size of this AI research corpus in [OpenAlex](https://openalex.org) through mid-2026, and **58.8% of it was published from 2023 through June 2026**. That window is three and a half years, not four. In 2025, **944,530** papers matched the query, a 42.6% rise over 2024 and a 10.1x increase since 2013. January through June 2026 logged **812,972**. Doubling that half-year gives about 1.6 million. Academic publishing is seasonal. 1.6 million is arithmetic, not a forecast.

Neural networks still dominate (**1,522,612 abstracts**, or 30.4% of the corpus). Large language models grew **29.9x** from 2018 to 2025, and every one of the ten fastest-rising keywords is LLM-related. China's **cumulative** count is 21.6% above the US. In 2025 the annual gap was **53.4%**. Nearly half of all papers (**48.9%**) have zero citations.

## I. Methodology (5 Million Papers, One Open API)

The corpus is **5,003,783** works published between 2013 and mid-2026, pulled from [OpenAlex](https://openalex.org) on **12 June 2026**. OpenAlex is a living index. Re-running the same strings later will not match digit-for-digit. The counts below are API totals for that pull, documented in the [SSRN paper](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=6991218).

The corpus is an abstract-level OR search on ten terms: *artificial intelligence, machine learning, deep learning, neural network, language model, reinforcement learning, computer vision, natural language, generative, autonomous.* A paper lands in the corpus if any of those strings appear in the abstract. That is a methods-mention census, not a roster of papers whose main contribution is AI. Abstract search returns **1.5x to 7.7x** more hits per keyword than title search in this pull. Those ratios are in the paper.

The resulting corpus is 65.4% journal articles, 13.4% preprints, and 7.7% book chapters. Repositories (primarily [arXiv](https://arxiv.org)) account for 27.4% of sources. Analyses are OpenAlex count queries. No full texts were downloaded.

## II. Keyword counts

The n-gram frequency analysis across 5,003,783 paper abstracts reveals the actual priorities of the global AI research enterprise. Not what conference keynotes claim matters, but what researchers are building.

  
  
  

**The bigram distribution splits cleanly into two tiers.** The top six terms are method-level. These are neural network, machine learning, deep learning, artificial intelligence, attention mechanism, and large language, totaling **5.37 million abstract mentions**. The bottom four are application-level. These are image classification, recommendation system, medical imaging, and feature extraction, totaling **1.39 million**. The ratio is 3.9 to 1. Method vocabulary dominates application vocabulary by nearly four to one.

**"Neural network"** (1,522,612 abstracts, 30.4% of the corpus) remains the foundation term. That is papers whose abstract contains the bigram, not 1.52 million unique architectures. The trend line is more useful than the cumulative stack. In 2025, **"deep learning" surpassed "neural network" in annual abstract mentions for the first time** (216,713 vs. 207,140), even as neural network retains the larger cumulative total.

**"Attention mechanism"** (432,079) at rank 5 confirms the transformer's structural dominance across NLP, computer vision, and multimodal tasks since 2017. **"Large language"** (405,166) at rank 6 has already surpassed application-oriented terms like image classification and recommendation systems, a crossover that occurred within the last two years.

### Trigram Architecture

The trigram distribution reveals the architectural building blocks of modern AI. **"Deep neural network"** (518,431) leads, followed by **"convolutional neural network"** (394,934). Together they account for over 913,000 abstract mentions.

The critical signal is that **"large language model"** (292,873) has overtaken both **"artificial neural network"** (261,355) and **"support vector machine"** (239,347) to claim the #3 position. LLMs are discussed far more broadly than title-only searches suggest. There are 292,873 abstract mentions versus just 71,469 title mentions, a 4.1x ratio. Five of the ten trigrams end in "network" (deep neural, convolutional neural, artificial neural, recurrent neural, graph neural), reflecting how many research areas have developed their own neural network variant.

## III. The LLM Inflection

The LLM trajectory represents the sharpest inflection in the entire five-million-paper corpus. No other term matches this acceleration profile.

**"Large language model"** abstract mentions grew from 3,248 in 2018 to 96,984 in 2025, a **29.9x increase**. The growth curve has a clear inflection point. Between 2018 and 2022, mentions grew at a modest pace (3,248 to 7,931, or 2.4x over four years). Between 2022 and 2025, they grew **12.2x in three years**. By 2025, abstracts mentioning "large language model" accounted for **10.3%** of that year's corpus papers (96,984 / 944,530), up from 1.9% in 2022. A naive annualization of the 2026 run-rate points at ~170,000. Same caveat as the headline 1.6 million: H2 is not a copy of H1.

For comparison, from 2022 to 2025 "transformer" grew 3.3x, "reinforcement learning" 2.7x, "deep learning" 2.1x, and "neural network" 1.5x. Nothing else comes close to the LLM growth rate.

### The Fastest-Rising Keywords

The ten fastest-rising keywords tell a definitive story about where research attention is shifting, and every single one is related to large language models. Not computer vision. Not reinforcement learning. Not graph methods. All LLM.

The data groups into three strategic categories.

1. **Named models as research subjects.** "DeepSeek" (848.7x), "Mistral" (16.8x), and "Gemini" (13.6x) are product names, not architectures. DeepSeek's multiple is a small-baseline explosion: 13 abstracts in 2022-2023, then 11,033 in 2025-2026. The ratio is real, not an 848x increase in model quality.

2. **The RAG pipeline.** "Retrieval augmented generation" (52.4x), "retrieval-augmented" (19.2x), and "RAG" (15.4x) collectively account for **58,494 papers** in 2025-2026, making RAG the single largest growth area by absolute volume after "LLM" itself. The enterprise has chosen its architecture. separate the reasoning engine from the knowledge store.

3. **Safety and reliability.** "Jailbreak" (25.5x) and "guardrail" (9.7x) track the growing research investment in making language models safe and reliable. This is no longer a niche concern. It is a research category with thousands of papers.

> 
"All ten of the fastest-rising keywords are related to large language models. None involve computer vision, reinforcement learning, or graph methods."

### Method Lifecycles

The time-series data places each value at a different lifecycle stage. Using the compound annual growth rate (CAGR) from 2022 to 2025 as the primary metric, with a corpus-wide baseline of 32.0%, we map 20 values onto an interpretive hype cycle.

- **Innovation trigger and ascending hype.** Chain of thought prompting (64.6% CAGR), coined in 2022, is the newest term. Vision language models (83.9% CAGR, 2,582 to 16,067 papers) and zero-shot learning (68.1%) grew in parallel with LLM adoption. RAG grew from 85 papers in 2022 to 9,329 in 2025 (378.8% CAGR, 110x), and is placed near the peak accordingly.
- **Peak of inflated expectations.** Large language models have the highest CAGR at 130.4% (7,931 to 96,984 papers). The annualized 2026 estimate (~170,000 papers) suggests continued growth.
- **Trough of disillusionment.** Vision transformers (60.9% CAGR) still show high growth but have moved from novelty to standard architecture since their 2021 peak. Diffusion models (33.9%) had their breakout in 2022-2023 and are now maturing. GANs (21.8%) and BERT (30.3%) have been largely superseded and sit deeper in the trough.
- **Slope of enlightenment.** Six values fall in this zone, all above the corpus average: multimodal learning (52.9%), federated learning (52.3%), transformers (48.8%), reinforcement learning (39.2%), contrastive learning (35.8%), and graph neural networks (33.2%). All show steady adoption past their initial growth phase.
- **Plateau of productivity.** Five values have below-average growth: deep learning (28.3% CAGR, 216,713 papers in 2025), knowledge graphs (25.9%), transfer learning (22.6%), CNNs (16.5%), and neural networks (15.4%). All continue to grow but at or below the corpus rate.

![Interpretive hype cycle for AI research terms. Growth rates shown are 2022-2025 CAGR (corpus average 32.0%).](/images/essays/fig_hype_cycle.png)

## IV. The Global Research Race

The geographic distribution of AI research has undergone a structural rebalancing. China now leads with **874,019 publications**, 21.6% more than the United States (718,676). The crossover occurred in 2021, when China produced 71,273 papers to the US's 64,931, and the gap has widened every year since.

The trajectory is striking. In 2013, the two countries started at near-parity (China with 12,074 and US with 13,829). Both grew steadily through 2018, but diverged sharply after that. US output actually declined slightly between 2021 and 2022 (64,931 to 64,486), while China accelerated. By 2025, the gap stood at **53.4%** (187,887 vs. 122,449).

The China-US gap is not uniform across research areas. China leads in six of seven term categories, strongest in "transformer" (2.67x) and "neural network" (1.87x). But the US retains the lead in the fastest-growing category. **"Large language model"** (47,363 vs. 35,923, or 1.32x). China reached LLM parity with the US only in 2025 (15,008 vs. 14,735).

### India

India ranks third globally with **369,931 publications**, and its growth trajectory is the steepest of any major producer. Indian AI research output grew **32.3x** from 2013 to 2025 (2,761 to 89,287 papers), a higher growth multiple than both China (15.6x) and the US (8.9x). In 2025, India produced more AI papers than Japan (15,558) and the UK (37,104) combined.

  
  
  

**Institutional concentration is significant.** The Chinese Academy of Sciences leads all institutions with 74,921 papers, 49.4% more than CNRS (50,145). Six of the top ten institutions globally are Chinese. Harvard (21,529) is the highest-ranked US institution at position 8.

Paper counts measure volume, not impact. OpenAlex assigns a paper to every co-author country, so China plus the US plus India can exceed 100% of the corpus. Citation-weighted metrics, top-1% shares, and venue prestige can rank the same countries differently. Read these figures as where abstracts are being written, not where the highest-impact work is produced.

## V. The Citation Economy

The citation distribution across five million AI papers follows an extreme power law. **48.9% of all papers have received zero citations.** Only 2,475 papers (0.05%) have exceeded 1,000 citations. The median paper in this AI corpus has zero citations.

This figure is partly inflated by recency. Papers published in 2024-2026 have had little time to accumulate citations. But the structural pattern is clear. A tiny fraction of papers captures the vast majority of research attention.

The most-cited paper in this pull is [ResNet](https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.03385) (He et al., 2015/2016) with **221,202** OpenAlex citations as of 12 June 2026, about 1.9x the next entry. Citation totals move. This is a snapshot. The top-cited papers share a common characteristic. They are reusable building blocks (ResNet, Adam, AlexNet, VGGNet, XGBoost). Infrastructure accumulates citations because every downstream paper that uses the tool cites the original.

> 
"More papers were published in 2025 alone (944,530) than in the first six years combined (2013-2018 at 734,197). The median paper has zero citations."

### Open Access Dominance

Of the 5,003,783 papers, **3,043,557 (60.8%)** are open access in OpenAlex's tagging. That is more than double the **28%** of Crossref-DOI journal articles [Piwowar et al. (2018)](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj.4375) found were OA across the whole literature. Their 28% is a 2018 snapshot of all fields, not a 2026 AI-specific control. The gap is still large. Preprint culture, anchored by arXiv, is the obvious driver.

## VI. Strategic Implications

The aggregation of 5,003,783 research papers yields three core strategic imperatives.

  
  
  

1. **The LLM wave is absorbing the rest of the stack.**
   LLMs grew 29.9x in seven years. Every one of the ten fastest-rising research keywords is LLM-related. RAG is the dominant deployment architecture. Organizations without LLM integration have already fallen behind. The strategic question is how to differentiate within an LLM-saturated research and product environment.

2. **Volume without impact is noise.**
   With 48.9% of papers receiving zero citations and only 0.05% exceeding 1,000, most of the pile is noise. Teams that can find the 0.05% inside the 944,000 papers published each year, and ignore the rest, have an advantage. The rest of the field is reading the same unread stack.

3. **The geography of AI leadership is multipolar.**
   China leads in volume. The US leads in LLMs. India is growing fastest. Six of the top ten institutions are Chinese, but the US retains disproportionate influence in the fastest-growing category. Any strategic assessment that treats "AI leadership" as a single dimension is incomplete. The competition is term-specific, institution-specific, and rapidly shifting.

*The query strings, tables, and caveats are in [State of AI Research (SSRN 6991218)](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=6991218). The live search tool is the [AI Reports Library](/ailib). Counts are the 12 June 2026 OpenAlex pull. They will drift.*

URL: https://veda.ng/stateofweb3
Summary: On 12 June 2026 OpenAlex tagged 128,286 blockchain papers. Yearly output grew 117 times from 2013 to 2025. A paper total is not a count of working software or of statutes in force.

## Three counts, not one field

A keyword jump can look like a boom. A tracker row can look like a currency that already exists. The June file is one tagged set of papers. It is not value locked, and it is not a list of currencies that exist.

The tagged set is 128,286 papers with those two OpenAlex tags, pulled on 12 June 2026. A wider abstract search in the same paper finds 1,938,409 papers. That is an upper bound, not the tagged set. Value locked, court dockets, statutes, CBDC trackers, and shipping platforms sit on a different meter. Abstract counts can rise while those stay put.

[Priem, Piwowar, and Orr (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.01833) built OpenAlex as an open replacement for Microsoft Academic Graph.

The yearly bars in the June chart add up to **127,286**. The tagged total is **128,286**. The paper does not explain the 1,000-record difference.

## What the papers were about, year by year

**2013 to 2016.** 176 to 955 papers. Most of the work was still [Nakamoto (2008)](https://bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf): stop double-spending without a bank. [Lamport, Shostak, and Pease (1982)](https://lamport.azurewebsites.net/pubs/byz.pdf) asked how generals agree when some messengers lie. Those four years in the chart sum to 2,111 papers, about five weeks of 2025 output.

**2017 to 2019.** 2017 grew 164% to 2,520. 2018 grew 178% to 6,995, the fastest year in the June file. [Buterin's Ethereum whitepaper](https://ethereum.org/en/whitepaper/) and [Wood's Yellow Paper](https://ethereum.github.io/yellowpaper/paper.pdf) turned a ledger into a computer that stores state. [Androulaki et al. (2018)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3190508.3190538) described Hyperledger Fabric for firms that wanted a chain only invited members can write to. By 2019 the yearly count was 10,591.

**2020 to now.** Growth slowed. 2024 grew 1.8%. Papers from 2020 through mid-2026 are 82.7% of the June file (106,069 of 128,286). The 2026 slice in that share is 8,419 papers seen by 12 June, not a full year. Ethereum's Merge on 15 September 2022 ended proof-of-work. The original Foundation post for that day is [gone](https://blog.ethereum.org/2022/09/15/the-merge-is-here). The live record is [ethereum.org/roadmap/merge](https://ethereum.org/roadmap/merge/). [ethereum.org's energy page](https://ethereum.org/en/energy-consumption/) cites CCRI: about 2,601 MWh a year after the switch (0.0026 TWh), a drop of more than 99.988% in electricity and about 99.992% in carbon against proof-of-work. Those are estimates, not an official Foundation promise. The comparison table on that page, with figures dated July 2023, puts Bitcoin at 149 TWh/yr, about 53,000 times proof-of-stake Ethereum. Bitcoin demand moves daily. The live index is the [Cambridge Bitcoin Electricity Consumption Index](https://ccaf.io/cbnsi/cbeci).

## Supply-chain papers kept rising after TradeLens shut down

"Blockchain" is in 68.5% of June abstracts (87,818). "Security" is in 46.3% (59,388). [Zheng, Xie, Dai, Chen, and Wang (2018)](https://doi.org/10.1504/IJWGS.2018.095647) listed failure modes early. [Khan and Salah (2018)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.future.2017.11.022) did the same for IoT. Security stayed in the abstracts. "Smart contract" is in 29.9% (38,414). "Bitcoin" is in 27.9%.

![Top two-word phrases in the June 2026 tagged set. Blockchain technology 44,102 (34.4%). Smart contract 21,134 (16.5%). Supply chain 11,418 (8.9%).](/images/essays/web3-terms.svg?v=3)

"Blockchain technology" (44,102) and "blockchain based" (18,516) are how authors add a ledger to some other system. "Supply chain" is the largest non-finance job at 11,418. [Saberi, Kouhizadeh, Sarkis, and Shen (2019)](https://doi.org/10.1080/00207543.2018.1533261) tied it to sustainability claims. [Christidis and Devetsikiotis (2016)](https://doi.org/10.1109/ACCESS.2016.2566339) tied it to IoT.

The largest industry test of that claim was TradeLens, a Maersk and IBM shipping platform announced in 2018. On 29 November 2022, [Maersk said it would shut the platform](https://www.maersk.com/news/articles/2022/11/29/maersk-and-ibm-to-discontinue-tradelens). The [19 December 2022 Wayback capture](https://web.archive.org/web/20221219103843/https://www.maersk.com/news/articles/2022/11/29/maersk-and-ibm-to-discontinue-tradelens) still has the text. The companies wrote that they had built a working platform, but "the need for full global industry collaboration has not been achieved," and it had not reached "the level of commercial viability necessary to continue work and meet the financial expectations as an independent business." The plan was to go offline by the end of Q1 2023. Supply-chain papers kept arriving after that. The tagged set still includes papers about products that later shut.

Health and privacy have early papers and smaller counts. [Zyskind, Nathan, and Pentland (2015)](https://doi.org/10.1109/SPW.2015.27) stored pointers to personal data, not the data. [Ekblaw, Azaria, Halamka, and Lippman](https://doi.org/10.1109/OBD.2016.11) built MedRec. "Healthcare" is in 13.7% of abstracts. "Machine learning" (5,667) plus "artificial intelligence" (5,463) is 11,130 mentions. [Kosba, Miller, Shi, Wen, and Papamanthou (2016)](https://doi.org/10.1109/SP.2016.55) hid contract internals (Hawk). [Lu, Huang, Zhang, Maharjan, and Zhang (2020)](https://doi.org/10.1109/TVT.2020.2973651) put federated learning on a ledger for vehicles. Mentions in 11,130 abstracts are not 11,130 working systems.

## DeFi papers rose while locked dollars split

DeFi mentions: 7 papers in 2019, 12 in 2020, 63 in 2021, **516 in 2025**. That is 74 times in six years. NFT mentions: 60 in 2021, **426 in 2023**, 334 in 2024, 366 in 2025.

![DeFi abstract mentions 7 in 2019 (0.07% of that year) to 516 in 2025 (2.5%). NFT mentions peaked at 426 in 2023 (2.4%).](/images/essays/web3-defi-nft.svg?v=3)

[Uniswap's docs](https://docs.uniswap.org) still describe the pool that replaced the order book. Live value locked is a different meter. [DefiLlama](https://defillama.com) is the public index. Its [2025 sector note](https://defillama.com/research/report/state-of-defi-2025) does not give one number for "DeFi." It splits:

- Lending TVL rose from $48.15 billion to $64.06 billion inside 2025. Top ten protocols held $57.00 billion, 89.0% of lending TVL.
- Liquid staking slipped from $58.73 billion to $57.62 billion.
- Restaking fell from $23.85 billion to $18.78 billion, a 21.2% drop.
- Tokenised US Treasuries and money-market products rose from $3.87 billion at end-2024 to $9.12 billion by late 2025.

A paper count can rise while some locked-dollar series rise and others fall.

The algorithmic stablecoin that blew up is in a court file. It is also in abstracts. On 16 February 2023 the [SEC charged Terraform Labs and Do Kwon](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2023-32) with a multi-billion-dollar securities fraud around UST, LUNA, and related tokens. Enforcement Director Gurbir S. Grewal said, as alleged, "the Terraform ecosystem was neither decentralized, nor finance." On 5 April 2024 a jury found them liable for securities fraud. On 13 June 2024 the [SEC announced a package above $4.5 billion](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-73): Terraform $3,586,875,883 disgorgement, $466,952,423 interest, $420 million penalty; Kwon $110 million disgorgement and $14,320,196 interest, joint and several with Terraform, plus an $80 million penalty. That release says the May 2022 de-peg "wiped out $40 billion in market value nearly overnight." Academics kept writing about DeFi after that. They wrote about reserved dollars and over-collateralized loans, not about UST.

NFT paper volume peaked in 2023, after the speculative market had already broken. Later papers are more about who owned an item than about profile pictures. The word stayed in abstracts after floor prices died.

Stablecoins already move money. The payment claim is smaller than the chain volume. [CoinDesk, citing McKinsey and Artemis](https://www.coindesk.com/business/2026/01/23/stablecoins-moved-usd35-trillion-last-year-but-only-1-of-it-was-for-real-world-payments) (23 January 2026), put 2025 on-chain stablecoin volume above $35 trillion. The same article prints **$390 billion** of "genuine" payments in the summary and **$380 billion** in the body ($226 billion B2B, $90 billion payroll and remittances, $8 billion capital markets). Those two figures do not match. Genuine payments are about 1% of the $35 trillion either way. McKinsey put the global payments market above $2 quadrillion, so even the higher figure is about 0.02% of that total. Circle and Tether still dominate issuance.

## Keywords that rose, and what actually shipped

Growth ratios in the June file compare 2025-2026 mentions to 2022-2023. A 6x jump off 37 papers is not the same as a 3x jump off 4,000.

![Fastest-rising terms in the June file, 2025-26 counts with growth vs 2022-23 in brackets. Quantum resistant 243 (+560%). Real world asset 89 (+460%). Layer 2 275 (+320%). zk rollup 34 (+240%).](/images/essays/web3-rising.svg?v=3)

**Post-quantum.** "Quantum resistant" grew 6.6x (37 to 243). "Post-quantum" grew 3.9x (95 to 367). Together, 610 papers in 2025-2026. Bitcoin and Ethereum still sign with elliptic curves. [Shor (1994)](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/9508027) showed a large quantum computer would break those signatures. There is no such machine on the public record. What moved the papers is a standards event. On 13 August 2024, [NIST published FIPS 203, 204, and 205](https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2024/08/nist-releases-first-3-finalized-post-quantum-encryption-standards). [FIPS 203](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/FIPS/NIST.FIPS.203.pdf) is ML-KEM. The [CSRC PQC page](https://csrc.nist.gov/groups/ST/post-quantum-crypto/) tells operators to start migrating. It does not give a date when ECDSA dies.

**Scale.** "Layer 2" grew 4.2x (275 papers). "zk rollup" grew 3.4x off **34** papers. The count rose, but 3.4x off 34 papers is not a volume story. [Buterin's 2021 rollup note](https://vitalik.eth.limo/general/2021/01/05/rollup.html) still describes the method: execute off the base chain, post data or a proof back. [L2BEAT](https://l2beat.com/scaling/summary) tracks live rollups. "Zero knowledge" grew 2.1x (743), the fastest rise among cryptographic primitives in the June file.

**Rules and tokens.** "Regulatory" grew 3.5x and the count is large: 4,529 papers. "Real world asset" grew 5.6x off 89 papers. "Stablecoin" grew 2.7x (576). "DeFi" grew 2.6x (808). "NFT" and "metaverse" sit at 0.8x.

[BlackRock launched BUIDL](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20240320771318/en) on Ethereum on 20 March 2024, a tokenized money-market fund for qualified investors, $5 million minimum, cash and Treasuries and repo, tokens targeting $1. Eighty-nine "real world asset" papers are not 89 copies of that fund. DefiLlama's tokenised-Treasury line ($3.87 billion to $9.12 billion in 2025) is closer to live dollars.

## EU and US rules arrived after the paper wave

The EU's [Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/1114/oj) (Regulation (EU) 2023/1114) was adopted on 31 May 2023 and published on 9 June 2023. It is the first EU-wide set of rules for issuance and crypto-asset services.

The US followed on stablecoins. The [GENIUS Act](https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/senate-bill/1582) became [Public Law 119-27 on 18 July 2025](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-119publ27/pdf/PLAW-119publ27.pdf). Payment stablecoins, 1:1 reserves. Signing remarks are in the [Daily Compilation](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/DCPD-202500778/html/DCPD-202500778.htm). The statute covers reserved dollars. It does not cover the algorithmic design the SEC sued.

Spot Bitcoin exchange-traded products were approved on 10 January 2024. [Chair Gensler's statement](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/speeches-statements/gensler-statement-spot-bitcoin-011023) is the public-market event. He wrote that the Commission did not approve bitcoin itself.

## 146 countries are on a CBDC tracker. Three have launched.

The [Atlantic Council tracker](https://www.atlanticcouncil.org/cbdctracker/) (May 2026) has 146 countries and currency unions with a CBDC entry, covering over 98% of world GDP, up from 87 in May 2022. 77 are in development, pilot, or launch. 41 pilots. Three retail CBDCs have launched: the Bahamas, Jamaica, and Nigeria. Every G20 member except the US is in the tracker. Canada, Australia, and Norway have stepped back from retail. The [BIS Innovation Hub CBDC page](https://www.bis.org/about/bisih/topics/cbdc.htm) covers the technical work. The [ECB digital euro page](https://www.ecb.europa.eu/euro/digital_euro/html/index.en.html) is the euro-area project. India's [RBI concept note](https://rbi.org.in/scripts/PublicationReportDetails.aspx?ID=1218) set out an e-rupee. CBDC papers in the June file go from 1 in 2016 to 205 in 2025. That follows official work. It is not 205 live currencies.

The tracker splits "launch" from "pilot." High volume and a launch label are not the same status.

| Tracker bucket (May 2026) | Count | What it is |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| In the tracker for a CBDC | 146 | Research through launch. 98% of world GDP. |
| Development, pilot, or launch | 77 | "Advanced" in the tracker. |
| Pilots | 41 | Includes e-CNY, the largest by volume. |
| Retail CBDCs fully launched | 3 | Bahamas, Jamaica, Nigeria. |

By December 2025, according to the same tracker, retail e-CNY had processed more than 3.4 billion transactions worth about 16.7 trillion yuan (~$2.3 trillion). In January 2026 the PBOC reclassified e-CNY as deposit liabilities. The Bahamas, Jamaica, and Nigeria are the three full launches. e-CNY has the most volume and still sits in the pilot column.

Nigeria launched eNaira in October 2021. The IMF's [May 2023 working paper](https://www.imf.org/-/media/files/publications/wp/2023/english/wpiea2023104-print-pdf.pdf) (WP/23/104) found about 14,000 transactions a week, 98.5% of wallets unused in a given week, and average weekly value of 923 million naira, 0.0018% of M3. The Fund called public adoption "disappointingly low." A later Article IV staff report, as quoted in [BusinessDay](https://businessday.ng/news/article/three-years-in-enaira-struggles-as-transactions-crawl-to-n29bn/), put cumulative transactions at 854,512 and N29.3 billion against N611 trillion of electronic payments in Nigeria in 2023.

China is the opposite case. Cryptocurrency trading is illegal. The [PBOC and nine other departments](https://www.pbc.gov.cn/tiaofasi/144941/3581332/4348658/index.html) issued 银发〔2021〕237号 in September 2021: virtual currency has no legal-tender status, related businesses are illegal financial activity, overseas exchanges serving mainland residents are also illegal. The [NDRC mining notice](https://www.gov.cn/zhengce/zhengceku/2021-09/25/content_5639225.htm) (发改运行〔2021〕1283号, 3 September 2021) ordered existing mines out and cut finance and power. The e-CNY is the state substitute. [Atlantic Council, 15 January 2026](https://www.atlanticcouncil.org/blogs/econographics/what-to-watch-as-china-prepares-its-digital-yuan-for-prime-time/), citing PBOC year-end data, matches the tracker on the 3.4 billion transactions and 16.7 trillion yuan. Project mBridge, after the BIS stepped back in October 2024, had processed about $55.49 billion, with e-CNY about 95% of settlement. That is a central bank payment system, not bitcoin.

The [Blockchain-based Service Network introductory whitepaper](https://bsnbase.io/static/tmpFile/BSNIntroductionWhitepaper.pdf) (5 February 2020) describes a network for government and firm chains that invited members write to. Chinese paper volume can be high while "Bitcoin" as a keyword is no longer the center. Inside China the legal topic is not a public coin.

## China and India write most of the papers. US products list in New York.

China 17,258 papers (13.5%). India 17,037 (13.3%). United States 12,488 (9.7%). Top three: 36.5% of the June file. In most computer-science fields the US is first or second. Here it is third.

![Country counts in the June file. China 17,258 (13.5%). India 17,037 (13.3%). United States 12,488 (9.7%). Indonesia 3,106 (2.4%).](/images/essays/web3-countries.svg?v=3)

OpenAlex assigns a paper to every co-author country, so shares can overlap. A paper with authors in China and the US counts in both.

The country split matches use more than it matches famous US universities. [Chainalysis's 2023 Global Crypto Adoption Index](https://www.chainalysis.com/blog/2023-global-crypto-adoption-index/) put India first in everyday use. Nigeria second, Vietnam third, the United States fourth. The [2023 geography report](https://www.chainalysis.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/the-2023-geography-of-cryptocurrency-report-release.pdf) put India second in raw estimated volume after the US, about $250 billion received in the year to June 2023. That was after [section 115BBH](https://incometaxindia.gov.in/Acts/Income-tax%20Act,%201961/2022/102120000000079592.htm) of the Income-tax Act (Finance Act 2022): 30% on transfer of a virtual digital asset, no expense other than cost of acquisition, no loss set-off. [Section 194S](https://www.incometaxindia.gov.in/w/section-194s-4) deducts 1% TDS. People used crypto anyway. Indonesia is rank 6 in the June paper file (3,106) and rank 7 on that adoption index. Saudi Arabia is rank 10 here (2,423).

No single US university sits in the top eight institutions in the June file. The [Chinese Academy of Sciences](https://english.cas.cn) has 924 papers. Indian Institutes of Technology occupy two of the top six slots. US work is spread. Paper volume is not a quality ranking. Citation-weighted lists can rank the same countries differently. The [State of AI essay](/stateofai) makes the same point on a five-million-paper pull.

China leads the paper count and bans the public coin. India is a close second in papers, first in everyday use, and taxes that use at 30%. The US is third in papers and first in the products that list on NYSE and Nasdaq.

  
  
  

## Most of these papers will not be cited

43.5% of the 128,286 papers have zero citations. 31.5% have 1 to 13. 20% have 14 to 41. 5% have 42 or more. The 99th percentile sits at 249. [Nakamoto (2008)](https://bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf) is an outlier at 14,286 OpenAlex citations in the June pull. [Zheng et al. (2017)](https://doi.org/10.1109/BigDataCongress.2017.85) is the survey a thousand later papers cite instead of citing the primary system. Melanie Swan's [2015 book](https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/blockchain-blueprint/9781491920480/) still collects citations. Most later "blockchain based X for Y" papers collect none.

![Citation split in the June file. 55,804 papers with zero citations (43.5%). 6,414 have 42 or more (5%).](/images/essays/web3-citations.svg?v=3)

82.7% of the tagged set is from 2020 on. New papers have had little time. Average citations per paper in the yearly file fall from 85.0 in 2013 to 0.8 in 2025. Most of this file will never be read twice.

## What the file counts

TradeLens shut after Maersk and IBM said it was not commercially viable. UST de-pegged in May 2022; the SEC later published a package above $4.5 billion. eNaira launched in 2021; the IMF found about 14,000 transactions a week and 98.5% of wallets unused. The June file still includes the papers written about each of them. It is 128,286 tagged works. 43.5% have zero citations. It is a literature pull, not a count of software that still runs.

China is 13.5% of that file and India is 13.3%. [MiCA](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/1114/oj) is the EU statute. The [GENIUS Act](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-119publ27/pdf/PLAW-119publ27.pdf) is the US payment-stablecoin statute. The same literature is searchable in the [Web3 Reports Library](/web3lib).

*The 12 June 2026 tables are in [Web3 Research Trends (SSRN 6990919)](https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6990919).*

## The Agent Infrastructure Stack
URL: https://veda.ng/agentstack
Summary: Over $5 billion in venture capital has been deployed into the eight layers of infrastructure that AI agents need to function.

In 2024 I built agents by gluing fifteen vendors together by hand: a model API, a headless browser, a scraper, a workflow engine, a vector store, evals, secrets, a sandbox. Each one wanted its own account and its own invoice. By mid-2026 you can pull most of that from one marketplace page with one bill. Vercel added an "Agents" category in 2025. Sixteen integrations now. Cloudflare hosts 78 models at the edge with function calling. HuggingFace Spaces is an app directory for ML. The picks-and-shovels shops behind that consolidation have raised more than $5 billion together.

![The Agent Infrastructure Stack: Eight layers of infrastructure, $5B+ in venture capital](/images/essays/agentstack.svg?v=2)

## How Agents See the Web

An autonomous agent that cannot read a webpage is blind. The perception layer converts the visual, interactive web into structured data that language models can process.

[Browserbase](https://www.browserbase.com/) provides headless browser infrastructure purpose-built for AI agents. It raised [$67.5 million](https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/browserbase) from Kleiner Perkins and CRV, reports over 50 million browser sessions served in 2025, and counts both Perplexity and Vercel among its customers. Rather than scraping HTML, Browserbase lets agents interact with websites the way a human would: clicking, scrolling, filling forms, and reading rendered content.

[Firecrawl](https://www.firecrawl.dev/) approaches perception differently. Instead of running a full browser session, it crawls URLs and converts them into clean, LLM-ready markdown. The company raised [$16.2 million](https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/firecrawl) through Y Combinator, and its output is now consumed by over 1 million developers, including teams at Apple, Canva, and Shopify. Where Browserbase provides interactive sessions, Firecrawl provides static extraction at scale.

Two newer entrants have emerged. [Parallel](https://www.parallel.ai/), founded by former Twitter CEO Parag Agrawal, raised [$230 million](https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/parallel-ai) across three rounds (most recently a $100 million Series B led by Sequoia at a $2 billion valuation) to build LLM-optimized web search and extraction APIs. [Kernel](https://kernel.sh/) raised [$22 million](https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/kernel-sh) (backed by Accel and Y Combinator) for browser-as-a-service infrastructure with sub-150ms spin-up times. And [Apify](https://apify.com/), the older player, runs 30,000+ pre-built web scrapers and generates $13.3 million in annual recurring revenue on only $3 million in external funding.

  - **$339M**: Combined funding into perception companies (Company disclosures, SEC filings)
  - **50M+**: Browserbase sessions served (2025) (Browserbase)
  - **1M+**: Developers using Firecrawl (Firecrawl)
  - **$2B**: Parallel valuation (Series B, Apr 2026) (Sequoia)

## How Agents Execute Multi-Step Tasks

A language model generates text. An orchestration engine turns that text into a sequence of durable, retryable actions that survive failures, timeouts, and restarts. Without orchestration, an agent that crashes mid-task has no way to resume.

[Temporal](https://temporal.io/) raised approximately [$650 million](https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/temporal-technologies) at a $5 billion valuation and operates the most widely adopted durable execution platform. OpenAI uses Temporal to run Codex. Snap, Netflix, and Stripe use it for backend workflows. It is infrastructure-heavy: self-hosted or cloud-hosted, designed for teams with dedicated platform engineers.

[Inngest](https://www.inngest.com/) raised approximately [$30 million](https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/inngest) from a16z and Altimeter and takes the opposite approach: serverless-first, zero-infrastructure orchestration that runs on Vercel and other platforms without dedicated ops teams. Its AgentKit product adds multi-agent coordination and human-in-the-loop approval flows, explicitly targeting the agent use case that Temporal serves more generally.

[Composio](https://composio.dev/) raised [$29 million](https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/composio) and provides a different kind of orchestration: tool integrations. Rather than managing execution state, Composio gives agents access to 100,000+ external tools (APIs, databases, SaaS products) through a single integration layer. Over 100,000 developers have adopted it.

## How Agents Are Measured

A chatbot that hallucinates costs you credibility. An agent that hallucinates costs you money. The evaluation layer exists because agents make decisions with real consequences, and the teams deploying them need to measure accuracy, latency, cost, and failure modes before those decisions hit production.

[Braintrust](https://www.braintrustdata.com/) raised over [$120 million](https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/braintrust-data) (at an $800 million valuation, led by ICONIQ) and provides evaluation, logging, tracing, and prompt management for AI applications. Stripe, Notion, and Airtable run their AI systems through Braintrust. It is listed on the Vercel Marketplace.

[Langfuse](https://langfuse.com/) took the open-source route. The company raised only [$4.5 million](https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/langfuse) before being acquired by ClickHouse in January 2026. By acquisition, 19 of the Fortune 50 were using it. The acquisition signals a pattern: observability is collapsing into database platforms.

[Arize AI](https://arize.com/) raised [$131 million](https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/arize-ai) and covers both traditional ML monitoring and LLM-specific evaluation. Booking.com, Uber, and Duolingo are customers. Where Braintrust focuses exclusively on LLM/agent evaluation, Arize spans the full ML stack.

One notable exit: [Helicone](https://helicone.ai/), an LLM observability proxy, was acquired by Mintlify in March 2026 and is now in maintenance mode.

## How Agents Think

Every agent call requires an inference pass. The compute layer provides the GPU infrastructure, model hosting, and API endpoints that turn prompts into responses. This is the largest value pool in the entire stack.

[Cerebras](https://cerebras.ai/) IPO'd on NASDAQ at $185 per share in May 2026 and trades at approximately $52 billion in market capitalization. It holds an OpenAI compute contract worth over $20 billion. The company builds custom wafer-scale chips designed for inference, not training, positioning it as purpose-built for the agentic workload pattern (many small, fast inference calls rather than months-long training runs).

[Together AI](https://www.together.ai/) raised approximately [$1.5 billion](https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/together-ai) at an $8.5 billion valuation, reports roughly $1 billion in annual recurring revenue, and provides both inference and open-source model training. [Modal](https://modal.com/) raised [$442 million](https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/modal-labs) at a $4.65 billion valuation and achieved 5x revenue growth in eight months during 2025-2026, hitting approximately $300 million ARR. [Fireworks AI](https://fireworks.ai/) raised over [$327 million](https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/fireworks-ai), processes more than 15 trillion tokens per day for customers including Samsung, Uber, and Cursor, and has grown to approximately $800 million ARR. The company is reportedly in discussions to raise at a $15 billion valuation. [Groq](https://groq.com/) raised approximately [$1.75 billion](https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/groq) for its custom LPU inference chips, and Nvidia subsequently licensed the LPU architecture for a reported $20 billion. Groq is now raising an additional $650 million and has undergone a leadership transition, with senior engineering talent departing to Nvidia following the licensing deal.

[fal.ai](https://fal.ai/) raised over [$400 million](https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/fal-ai) (most recently a $140 million Series D led by Sequoia at a $4.5 billion valuation) for serverless media generation infrastructure. Adobe, Canva, Shopify, and Perplexity are customers. fal processes billions of generative assets monthly across 600+ models. The company is reportedly in discussions to raise $300 to $350 million more at approximately $8 billion.

And then there is Cloudflare. Workers AI hosts a [rotating catalog of 50+ production models](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers-ai/models/) from Meta, Google, OpenAI, Qwen, Mistral, NVIDIA, and others, with function calling, LoRA fine-tuning, vision inputs, and batch processing built in. Older models are regularly deprecated as newer architectures arrive. A CDN company running inference at 300+ edge locations globally represents a structural change in how compute is distributed, moving from centralized GPU clusters to the edge, closer to the applications that consume it.

## How Agents Remember

A stateless agent forgets everything between calls. Memory infrastructure provides persistent context, including what the agent has done, what the user prefers, and what documents are relevant to the current task.

[Mem0](https://www.mem0.ai/) raised [$24 million](https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/mem0) and provides memory management purpose-built for AI agents and assistants. It is the exclusive memory provider in the [AWS Agent SDK](https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/agents/).

[Upstash](https://upstash.com/) raised [$11.9 million](https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/upstash) from a16z and provides serverless Redis, Kafka, and vector storage. It sits on the Vercel Marketplace and is widely used for session state, rate limiting, and lightweight vector search in agent architectures.

For retrieval, the vector database category attracted heavy funding in 2022-2023 and has been quiet since. [Pinecone](https://www.pinecone.io/) raised [$138 million](https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/pinecone) and reports 9,000+ customers and 800,000 developers. [Qdrant](https://qdrant.tech/) raised [$87.8 million](https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/qdrant) (the only vector database to raise a new round since 2023) and counts Disney, Microsoft, and Deloitte as customers. [Weaviate](https://weaviate.io/) raised [$67.7 million](https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/weaviate). [Chroma](https://www.trychroma.com/) raised [$18 million](https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/chroma-ai). The funding pause suggests either market saturation or a recognition that vector search is becoming a feature of general-purpose databases (Postgres with pgvector, Redis with vector modules) rather than a standalone category.

## How Agents Run Code Safely

An agent that writes code needs somewhere to run it. Executing untrusted, LLM-generated code on your production servers is a security breach waiting to happen. The sandboxed execution layer provides isolated environments where agents can run arbitrary code without risk.

[E2B](https://e2b.dev/) raised [$32 million](https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/e2b-dev) and provides cloud-based sandboxed environments (micro-VMs) specifically designed for AI-generated code execution. Hugging Face, Perplexity, and Groq integrate E2B into their products, and the company reports that 88% of Fortune 100 companies have signed up. Each sandbox is an isolated, ephemeral micro-VM with its own filesystem, network, and process tree, created on demand and destroyed when the task completes.

## How Agents Are Defended

The security layer has undergone the fastest consolidation in the entire stack. Three of four pure-play agent security companies were acquired within eighteen months.

[Lakera](https://www.lakera.ai/), which built prompt injection detection, raised [$30 million](https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/lakera) and was [acquired by Check Point](https://www.checkpoint.com/press-releases/check-point-acquires-lakera/) for approximately $300 million in September 2025. [Robust Intelligence](https://www.robustintelligence.com/), which built AI model validation, raised [$44 million](https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/robust-intelligence) and was [acquired by Cisco](https://blogs.cisco.com/security/cisco-acquires-robust-intelligence) in October 2024. [Galileo AI](https://www.rungalileo.io/), which built LLM hallucination detection, raised [$68 million](https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/galileo-ai) and was [acquired by Cisco](https://blogs.cisco.com/security/cisco-acquires-galileo) in April 2026. Cisco alone absorbed two agent security companies in eighteen months.

The sole independent survivor is [Patronus AI](https://www.patronus.ai/), which raised [$40 million](https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/patronus-ai) at approximately $80.5 million valuation.

Two newer security entrants are approaching the problem differently. [Corridor](https://corridor.dev/) raised [$30.4 million](https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/corridor-security) (including a $25 million Series A at $200 million valuation) for "agentic coding security," scanning PRs generated by AI coding agents for vulnerabilities. Its founders (Jack Cable and Ashwin Ramaswami) came from CISA, the federal cybersecurity agency. [Arcjet](https://arcjet.com/) raised [$12.1 million](https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/arcjet) for in-code rate limiting and bot protection, embedding security directly into application logic rather than sitting at the network perimeter. [Descope](https://www.descope.com/) raised [$88 million](https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/descope) for authentication infrastructure that now includes an Agentic Identity Hub with OAuth 2.1 for AI agents, used by Databricks, MongoDB, and GoodRx.

Standalone agent security is being absorbed into larger platform companies (Cisco, Check Point), while the next generation of security companies are embedding themselves directly into the developer workflow. In late May 2026, Palo Alto Networks acquired Portkey, an AI gateway company, to add agent runtime security and identity to its Prisma AIRS platform. Snowflake acquired Natoma, an MCP platform for agent governance. Asana acquired Stack AI, a no-code agent builder, for approximately $75 million. The acquirer profile is expanding beyond security vendors to include data platforms and productivity companies.

## Who Ships Autonomous Agents

The infrastructure stack exists to support the companies that ship agents as finished products. The valuations at this layer dwarf every infrastructure category combined.

[Cognition](https://cognition.ai/) (Devin) has raised over [$2.5 billion](https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/cognition-ai) at a $26 billion valuation and reports $492 million in annual recurring revenue from its autonomous software engineering agent. [Sierra AI](https://sierra.ai/), co-founded by former Salesforce CEO Bret Taylor, raised approximately [$1.58 billion](https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/sierra-ai) at a $15.8 billion valuation for customer experience agents deployed by WeightWatchers, ADT, and Sonos, reaching $150 million ARR within its first eight quarters. [Harvey AI](https://www.harvey.ai/) raised over [$1.22 billion](https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/harvey-ai) at an $11 billion valuation for legal agents, with 25,000+ agents running on its platform. [Decagon](https://decagon.ai/) raised approximately [$481 million](https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/decagon-ai) at a $4.5 billion valuation for customer support agents used by Cash App, Notion, and Duolingo. [Factory AI](https://factory.ai/) raised approximately [$200 million](https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/factory-ai) at a $1.5 billion valuation for software development agents used by NVIDIA, Adobe, and MongoDB. [CodeRabbit](https://coderabbit.ai/) raised [$88 million](https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/coderabbit) at a $550 million valuation, operates the #1 AI application on the GitHub Marketplace, and has over 8,000 paying organizations.

Combined, these six companies represent over $59 billion in valuation on roughly $6 billion in capital raised. The coding vertical alone (Cognition + Factory + CodeRabbit) accounts for $28 billion.

## What Funding Data Reveals About Agent Infrastructure

![Agentic AI funding: $1.5B (2024) to $2.9B (2025), top 10 deals capture 78% of capital](/images/essays/agent-funding-landscape.svg?v=1)

Disclosed equity funding for pure-play agentic AI companies nearly doubled from $1.5 billion in 2024 to $2.9 billion in 2025. The number of disclosed deals grew from 31 to 50. Between January and May 2026, the market raised another $1.1 billion across 29 deals, putting it on pace for approximately $2.6 billion annualized. The raw capital growth is real. What the headline numbers obscure is where that capital actually lands.

### Capital Concentrates Violently

The distribution is not normal. In early 2026, the top 3 deals captured 44% of total agentic AI capital. The top 10 captured 78%. The bottom half of all deals split 11.5% among themselves. This is the defining structural feature of the agent funding market. A small number of companies absorb most of the money, and the rest compete for scraps.

This concentration exists at every stage. The median AI seed round in 2026 sits at approximately $4.6 million, up from around $3 million for the broader market. But the upper quartile of AI seed deals now exceeds $8 to $10 million, and outlier rounds (Parallel's $30 million seed, for example) distort the average further. Investors increasingly expect $500K to $1 million in ARR at seed stage, a bar that would have been Series A territory three years ago.

At Series A and beyond, the bar is higher still. Investors are moving away from generic agent builders toward "control planes" and "operating systems" for agents, companies that lock in durable workflow integration. The shift from 2025 to 2026 is visible. 2025 was dominated by mega-rounds for foundation model companies. 2026 is more deal-driven, with renewed interest in the operating stack required to deploy agents safely.

### Who Is Funding What

The investor thesis splits along clear lines. Sequoia leads growth-stage rounds for vertical agents (Sierra) and compute (fal.ai), with a newer bet on perception (Parallel). a16z funds horizontal infrastructure, including orchestration (Inngest), storage (Upstash), and the development environments that agents run in. Kleiner Perkins straddles both, leading the largest perception deal (Browserbase at $67.5M) while backing vertical players like Harvey and Glean. Y Combinator operates as the primary seed pipeline for agent infrastructure, with Firecrawl, Kernel, E2B, Cubic, and Meticulous all passing through its batches.

The geographic distribution is lopsided. The United States captures approximately 82% of all agentic AI venture capital. Europe accounts for roughly 10 to 12%, with France (Mistral), the UK, and Germany producing the majority of European agent companies. Israel punches above its weight in agent security specifically (Robust Intelligence, Patronus AI). India and Southeast Asia remain underrepresented in the infrastructure layer, though vertical agent companies in healthcare and fintech are growing in both regions.

### What the Category Split Looks Like

Funding data segments the market into three broad categories. Vertical AI agents, companies building agents for specific industries (legal, healthcare, customer support, coding), accounted for approximately 55% of agentic AI capital and 48% of deals in early 2026. Agent execution infrastructure, the picks-and-shovels layer, drew a smaller share of total dollars but showed the highest growth rate in deal count. Agent development platforms (orchestration, frameworks, SDKs) experienced fluctuations throughout 2025 but rebounded in 2026 as teams moved from prototype to production.

The pattern aligns with what the company-level data shows. Vertical agents attract the biggest checks (Cognition, Harvey, Sierra), while infrastructure companies raise smaller rounds but grow faster in deal volume. Investors are placing large bets on a few vertical winners while spreading smaller bets across the infrastructure stack, hedging on which layers will consolidate.

### The Failure Rate Nobody Discusses

Industry analysts estimate that 80 to 90% of early-stage AI agent startups face closure or consolidation during the current shakeout. The primary failure mode is thin wrappers around foundation model APIs. Companies that offer single-purpose tools with no proprietary model, data, or workflow advantage are being commoditized by the model providers themselves. OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google are shipping native features (function calling, tool use, code execution) that eliminate the value proposition of dozens of wrapper startups simultaneously.

The companies that survive share a common trait. They own a piece of the workflow that the model provider cannot replicate. Browserbase owns the browser session. E2B owns the sandbox. Temporal owns the execution state. Inngest owns the serverless orchestration layer. Braintrust owns the evaluation data. None of these can be replaced by adding a feature to GPT-5.

### The M&A Signal

Twelve acquisitions in the agent infrastructure space between October 2024 and May 2026 reveal where platform companies see gaps. Cisco acquired both Robust Intelligence and Galileo AI, spending over $400 million to build an agent security division. Check Point acquired Lakera for approximately $300 million. IBM acquired Confluent for $11 billion (real-time data streaming for agents) and HashiCorp for $6.4 billion (infrastructure provisioning). Meta acquired Manus for approximately $2 billion (autonomous agent platform). ClickHouse acquired Langfuse (open-source observability). Mintlify acquired Helicone (observability proxy). In late May 2026, three more followed in rapid succession. Palo Alto Networks acquired Portkey (AI gateway and agent governance). Snowflake acquired Natoma (MCP-based agent governance). Asana acquired Stack AI (no-code agent platform, approximately $75 million).

The acquirers are Cisco, IBM, Meta, Check Point, Palo Alto Networks, Snowflake, and Asana, infrastructure incumbents and platform companies that missed the initial agent wave and are buying their way in. Security, observability, and data infrastructure companies get acquired. Compute and perception companies do not, because those layers are harder to replicate through acquisition. The acquirer profile is also widening. Where 2024-2025 acquisitions came from security and infrastructure vendors, 2026 brought data platforms (Snowflake) and productivity tools (Asana) into the mix.

### The Bootstrapped Counterexample

Not every successful agent company raised venture capital. [Chatbase](https://www.chatbase.co/) reached $10 million ARR with 8,000 to 10,000 paying customers and 18 employees, entirely bootstrapped. [Apify](https://apify.com/) generates $13.3 million ARR on only $3 million in external funding. [DebugBear](https://debugbear.com/), a web performance monitoring tool on the Vercel Marketplace, serves 2,000+ customers and was primarily bootstrapped with a TinySeed accelerator investment. These companies share a trait: they sell to individual developers and small teams with credit-card-accessible pricing, avoiding the enterprise sales cycle that burns cash.

The bootstrapped path works for tools in the perception, monitoring, and developer experience layers. It does not work for compute (capital-intensive), security (enterprise sales required), or orchestration (infrastructure complexity). The funding data confirms the obvious. Some layers require venture capital to exist, and others can be built profitably from day one.

## Developer Platforms Are Productizing the Stack

The clearest evidence that agent infrastructure has matured from GitHub repositories to managed services is the Vercel Marketplace. It contains 97+ integrations across 22 categories. The "Agents" category, added in 2025, now includes Browserbase, Firecrawl, Braintrust, CodeRabbit, Inngest, Parallel, Profound, Corridor, and others. Each can be provisioned with one click, billed through a single invoice, and connected to a Vercel project with automatic API key injection.

![Vercel Marketplace: 97+ integrations across 22 categories](/images/essays/vercel-marketplace-map.svg?v=10)

Vercel is one marketplace among several. Cloudflare Workers AI serves 50+ production models at the edge with OpenAI-compatible endpoints. HuggingFace Spaces operates as the largest ML application directory. LangChain's LangSmith provides a hub for reusable agent chains, prompts, and evaluation datasets. The infrastructure stack is being absorbed into platforms the same way databases, storage, and compute were absorbed into AWS in the 2010s.

Two companies from the Vercel Marketplace illustrate how quickly new categories form. [Profound](https://www.profound.com/), which monitors how brands appear in AI-generated search results (ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google AI Overviews), reached unicorn status ($1 billion valuation on $155 million raised) within 18 months of founding.

## What the Data Shows

Security got bought. Vector DBs stopped raising. Coding agents carry the largest product valuations. Inference is the capital sink. The open question is whether the layers stay independent or collapse into one bill, the way AWS absorbed the rest.
